#34836. How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 12 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation.
  • In a recent development, since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests.
  • According to recent reports, this sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation. In short: for the first output token (prefill step), the entire prompt needs to be processed, which can be parallelized efficiently and can saturate GPU utilization. For all later output tokens (decode steps), only a single additional token needs to be processed, which is less compute-intensive but must be done sequentially. When many requests are processed concurrently, any strategy that aims for low latency needs to run prefill steps for newly arriving requests while the decode steps of previously scheduled requests are still ongoing. Concurrent processing of new as well as running requests therefore requires careful balancing between the prefill and decode stages, which presents two major challenges, which we will discuss in the following. One is a readily solvable glitch, while the other one constitutes a more fundamental flaw.

In a recent development, since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests. For prefill, however, this approach does not work. Because of the parallelized processing of all prompt tokens, a single prefill step can already saturate GPU utilization. Consequently, in the default chunked-prefill strategy of vLLM, each prefill chunk contains only prompt tokens of a single request. The next request in line has to wait until the previous prefill phase has been finished before its own prefill phase can start.

According to recent reports, this sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue. (Note that the sequential processing of prefills is the default characteristic of chunked-prefill and only appears when there already is a concurrent request in its decode phase; hence the name "partial prefill".).

Unfortunately, this challenge can neither be solved with vLLM-side priority scheduling (see the first article of this series) nor with a more sophisticated upstream scheduler. The reason is that the long prompt can be scheduled before any subsequent requests exist, so there is nothing the scheduler could wait for.

A straightforward solution would be to process prefill chunks of different requests in parallel. This might not be resource-optimized, as single-request prefill chunks could already saturate compute-power. Any additional prefill executed in parallel would likely prolong the prefill duration a bit and slow down any concurrent decode-requests even further. This would be acceptable if it reduced the latency of short requests and made the system appear more responsive. This approach fails, however, when the next request in line has a long prompt too. In such a case, two compute-intensive prefills would be batched together and result in a severe slowdown.

In a recent development, in one of the latest vLLM updates, an improved strategy has been implemented: it allows for parallel prefills of different requests but with a limit to the number of concurrently processed long prompt requests. An example configuration could enable batching of prefills for four requests, but only one of them may be longer than 10,000 prompt tokens. With such a configuration, the behavior for longer requests is still the same as before: long prompts are processed sequentially. Short requests, however, no longer need to wait for the long prefill of a previous request to finish; short prompts can take a fast lane. These requests no longer suffer from long waiting times and show much lower time-to-first-token metrics.

Sources indicate that of course, parallel prefills can only reduce waiting times; but the time-per-output-token remains elevated during the concurrent long-prefill operation. In this regard, request-parallel prefills show the same behavior and performance as standard chunked-prefill, just with a shorter time-to-first-token.

Whenever prefill and decode of different requests are executed in the same GPU operation, it takes longer than for an isolated decode step. The user experiences an interruption or a slowing down of the token generation by a subsequent request. In particular, a single request with a long prompt is sufficient to slow down all previously scheduled requests that are already in their decode phases.

This is a fundamental flaw in the concurrent processing of prefill and decode on the same GPUs, because there is little you can do:.

The difference between ideal concurrent processing (which would be no different from isolated requests), actual concurrent processing, and a disaggregated prefill strategy is shown by the following measurements:.

Separating prefill and decode eliminates the slowing-down of token generation in presence of other requests to a large extent, which makes it a very attractive strategy. It comes at the price of a second full-size vLLM deployment (e.g. for Llama-3.3-70B, you would need four H100 GPUs for a prefill worker and another four H100 GPUs for a decode worker if you wanted to support a maximum context length of 130k tokens). Another disadvantage is the uneven GPU utilization: because prefill is compute-intensive but decode is not, the prefill worker will likely saturate GPU utilization before the decode worker does. On the other hand, large clusters could consist of different numbers of prefill and decode workers (depending on load patterns), in order to optimize resource utilization.

It has been revealed that disaggregated prefill is not intended to increase total throughput, rather total "goodput" (i.e. the rate of requests that satisfy latency targets). Consequently, it is not the best use of GPU resources if your application is not sensitive to latency of individual requests.

Industry observers note that another caveat: the disaggregated prefill feature in vLLM is still experimental, and some optimizations and features are not accessible yet. For example, there are right now lower limits on context length, and the decode worker doesn't use CUDA graphs consistently, causing the slower decode of the long-prompt request in the figure above. Fortunately, these are not fundamental obstacles and are likely going to be solved in future versions of vLLM.

SSDs, laptops, and phones may get cheaper as consumer NAND spot pricing drops 20%

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years.
  • It has been revealed that the report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month.
  • SED notes that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years. Beyond the stratospheric prices of DDR5 memory, prospective PC builders and consumer electronics buyers have had to deal with upcharges on SSDs of all sizes thanks to the AI boom. That may be changing soon, as spot pricing for consumer NAND chips is reportedly dropping, according to a upcoming report from Seoul Economic Daily (SED).

It has been revealed that the report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month. Its conclusions are bolstered by information from a Bank of America note from Nov. 13, wherein industry sources tell that institution that NAND is due for a market correction.

SED notes that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90. SED quotes another industry source that says: "NAND cannot sustain the steep price gains seen so far.".

Those decreases may be hard to square in a time when enterprise SSDs are getting pricier by the day, but SED notes that the rise in phone and PC prices has led customers to delay upgrades, resulting in a 20% year-on-year decline in shipments for phones alone and making for the lowest third-quarter volumes in 14 years. Meanwhile, PC shipments have also fallen 22.5% year-on-year, according to a Gartner report.

In the face of those consumer decisions, device makers are letting their existing stock drain out and are presumably stocked with NAND chips for the short term, thus resulting in lower prices for new fab shipments on the short-term spot market.

Another factor in the consumer NAND market is that not all flash is equal. Both RAM and NAND makers have been redirecting their chip output to serve the ongoing AI boom, converting their consumer-grade production lines to make higher-spec silicon. Memory factories have been converting DDR5 capacity to HBM at a steady pace, as parts of the process are shared across both types.

But according to the Bank of America note that SED cites, things are different in the NAND world. High-density flash now sits at around 300 layers, and its production requires substantially different tooling compared to the lower-grade silicon deemed suitable for us mere mortals. So the continuing growth in NAND demand from AI data centers may not translate directly into reduced consumer supply.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Beyond those factors, added supply from Chinese NAND maker YMTC is creating additional downward price pressure in the NAND market. SED notes that YMTC has taken a 14% chunk from major players in the NAND market in the second quarter of this year alone.

It has been revealed that on net, these forces could result in a bit of relief for consumer tech. SED says Bank of America expects consumer NAND prices for PCs and smartphones to fall 5% to 10% on the longer-term contract market in the first quarter of 2027, while enterprise NAND contract prices are expected to hold more or less steady.

It has been revealed that whether those declines translate to lower prices for finished devices and components like SSDs will remain to be seen, and products with those chips inside will require some time to reach the market. But in the ongoing AI supply crunch, any potential relief is worth celebrating.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we're thrilled to share that Groq is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!
  • Groq supports a wide variety of text and conversational models, including the latest open-source models such as Meta's Llama 4, Qwen's QWQ-32B, and many more.
  • At the heart of Groq's technology is the Language Processing Unit (LPU™), a fresh type of end-to-end processing unit system that provides the fastest inference for computationally intensive applications with a sequential component, such as Large Language Models (LLMs).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we're thrilled to share that Groq is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub! Groq joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub’s model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Groq supports a wide variety of text and conversational models, including the latest open-source models such as Meta's Llama 4, Qwen's QWQ-32B, and many more.

At the heart of Groq's technology is the Language Processing Unit (LPU™), a fresh type of end-to-end processing unit system that provides the fastest inference for computationally intensive applications with a sequential component, such as Large Language Models (LLMs). LPUs are designed to overcome the limitations of GPUs for inference, offering significantly lower latency and higher throughput. This makes them ideal for real-time AI applications.

Sources indicate that groq offers fast AI inference for openly-available models. They provide an API that allows developers to easily integrate these models into their applications. It offers an on-demand, pay-as-you-go model for accessing a wide range of openly-available LLMs.

Sources indicate that you can now use Groq's Inference API as an Inference Provider on Huggingface. We're quite excited to see what you'll build with this newly introduced provider.

Read more about how to use Groq as Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

See the list of supported models here.

The following example demonstrates how to use Meta's Llama 4 using Groq as the inference provider. You can use a Hugging Face token for automatic routing through Hugging Face, or your own Groq API key if you have one.

Install huggingface_hub from source (see instructions). Official support will be released soon in version v0.33.0.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Groq API key you're billed on your Groq account.

Recent findings suggest that for routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us, we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

Notable Note ‼️ PRO customers get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥.

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free users, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

We would love to get your feedback! Share your thoughts and/or comments here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49.

Groq’s integration as an Inference Provider on Hugging Face delivers ultra‑low latency and high‑throughput LPU‑powered inference for cutting‑edge open‑source LLMs — a game‑changer for real‑time AI deployments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance.
  • Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them.
  • We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance. We saw how bitsandbytes, torchao, and others reduce memory footprints for generating images.

Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them. Therefore, in this post, we tackle efficient fine-tuning of these models with peak memory use under ~10 GB of VRAM on a single GPU. This post will guide you through fine-tuning FLUX.1-dev using QLoRA with the diffusers library. We'll showcase results from an NVIDIA RTX 4090. We'll also highlight how FP8 training with torchao can further optimize speed on compatible hardware.

We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.

The model consists of three main components:.

In our QLoRA approach, we focus exclusively on fine-tuning the transformer component. The text encoders and VAE remain frozen throughout training.

Industry observers note that we used a diffusers training script (slightly modified from here designed for DreamBooth-style LoRA fine-tuning of FLUX models. Also, a shortened version to reproduce the results in this blogpost (and used in the Google Colab) is available here. Let's examine the crucial parts for QLoRA and memory efficiency:.

Recent findings suggest that loRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) Deep Dive: LoRA makes model training more efficient by keeping track of the weight updates with low-rank matrices. Instead of updating the full weight matrix W W W, LoRA learns two smaller matrices A A A and B B B. The update to the weights for the model is ΔW=BA \Delta W = B A ΔW=BA, where A∈Rr×k A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k} A∈Rr×k and B∈Rd×r B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r} B∈Rd×r. The number r r r (called rank) is much smaller than the original dimensions, which means less parameters to update. Lastly, α \alpha α is a scaling factor for the LoRA activations. This affects how much LoRA affects the updates, and is often set to the same value as the r r r or a multiple of it. It helps balance the influence of the pre-trained model and the LoRA adapter. For a general introduction to the concept, check out our previous blog post: Using LoRA for Efficient Stable Diffusion Fine-Tuning.

QLoRA: The Efficiency Powerhouse: QLoRA enhances LoRA by first loading the pre-trained base model in a quantized format (typically 4-bit via bitsandbytes), drastically cutting the base model's memory footprint. It then trains LoRA adapters (usually in FP16/BF16) on top of this quantized base. This dramatically lowers the VRAM needed to hold the base model.

In a recent development, for instance, in the DreamBooth training script for HiDream 4-bit quantization with bitsandbytes reduces the peak memory usage of a LoRA fine-tune from ~60GB down to ~37GB with negligible-to-none quality degradation. The very same principle is what we apply here to fine-tune FLUX.1 on a consumer-grade hardware.

8-bit Optimizer (AdamW): Standard AdamW optimizer maintains first and second moment estimates for each parameter in 32-bit (FP32), which consumes a lot of memory. The 8-bit AdamW uses block-wise quantization to store optimizer states in 8-bit precision, while maintaining training stability. This technique can reduce optimizer memory usage by ~75% compared to standard FP32 AdamW. Enabling it in the script is straightforward:.

In a recent development, gradient Checkpointing: During forward pass, intermediate activations are typically stored for backward pass gradient computation. Gradient checkpointing trades computation for memory by only storing certain checkpoint activations and recomputing others during backpropagation.

Cache Latents: This optimization technique pre-processes all training images through the VAE encoder before the beginning of the training. It stores the resulting latent representations in memory. During the training, instead of encoding images on-the-fly, the cached latents are directly used. This approach offers two main benefits:.

Only these LoRA parameters become trainable.

Before we launch the QLoRA fine-tune we can save a huge chunk of VRAM and wall-clock time by caching outputs of text encoders once.

At training time the dataloader simply reads the cached embeddings instead of re-encoding the caption, so the CLIP/T5 encoder never has to sit in GPU memory.

By combining this with cached VAE latents (--cache_latents) you whittle the active model down to just the quantized transformer + LoRA adapters, keeping the whole fine-tune comfortably under 10 GB of GPU memory.

For this demonstration, we leveraged an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM) to explore its performance. The full training command using accelerate is shown below.

It has been revealed that configuration for RTX 4090: On our RTX 4090, we used a train_batch_size of 1, gradient_accumulation_steps of 4, mixed_precision="bf16", gradient_checkpointing=True, use_8bit_adam=True, a LoRA rank of 4, and resolution of 512x768. Latents were cached with cache_latents=True.

Training Time (RTX 4090): Fine-tuning for 700 steps on the Alphonse Mucha dataset took approximately 41 minutes on the RTX 4090 with train_batch_size of 1 and resolution of 512x768.

According to recent reports, the fine-tuned model nicely captured Mucha's iconic art nouveau style, evident in the decorative motifs and distinct color palette. The QLoRA process maintained excellent fidelity while learning the new style.

For users with NVIDIA GPUs possessing compute capability 8.9 or greater (such as the H100, RTX 4090), even greater speed efficiencies can be achieved by leveraging FP8 training via the torchao library.

After training your LoRA adapters, you have two main approaches for inference.

One approach is to load your trained LoRA adapters on top of the base model.

For when you want maximum efficiency with a single style, you can merge the LoRA weights into the base model.

While we showcased results on an RTX 4090, the same code can be run on more accessible hardware like the T4 GPU available in Google Colab for free.

On a T4, you can expect the fine-tuning process to take significantly longer around 4 hours for the same number of steps. This is a trade-off for accessibility, but it makes custom fine-tuning possible without high-end hardware. Be mindful of usage limits if running on Colab, as a 4-hour training run might push them.

According to recent reports, QLoRA, coupled with the diffusers library, significantly democratizes the ability to customize state-of-the-art models like FLUX.1-dev. As demonstrated on an RTX 4090, efficient fine-tuning is well within reach, yielding high-quality stylistic adaptations. Furthermore, for users with the latest NVIDIA hardware, torchao enables even faster training through FP8 precision.

Sharing your fine-tuned LoRA adapters is a fantastic way to contribute to the open-source community. It allows others to easily try out your styles, build on your work, and helps create a vibrant ecosystem of creative AI tools.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today.
  • There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat.
  • It has been revealed that these are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today. A countdown at Orbital Radar confirmed that Voyager cruised past the threshold at a leisurely 37,844 mph just after 5 am ET on Wednesday, November 18. It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.

There are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat. Sci-fi highlights casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store. One light-day isn’t a distance to be derided, though. Over the last half century, hurtling through space at a cruising speed of 38,000 mph, the Voyager spacecraft has clocked about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers).

It has been revealed that these are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming. So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds. For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth. Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet. Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds. Now let us remind you that Voyager 1 is on the brink of being a whole light-day away.

Industry observers note that on Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over. NASA claims that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor. We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record. Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists rolled out Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message. Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet.

If an alien got hold of the record on Wednesday and managed to rustle up a gramophone player to listen to it, a message sent to Earth via radio waves would take a full 24 hours to be received.

Space enthusiasts are also invited to participate in a global event “by creating a wave of golden light.” It sounds rather pointless, but enthusiasts are asked to flash the three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, into the night sky - Morse Code style - using their phone flashlights. There’s a website you can open to flash your screen appropriately.

  • It has been revealed that ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know.
  • Whatever you're building, the fix is the same: stop trusting the model with the parts it can get wrong, and check its work before anyone sees it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

It has been revealed that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

It has been revealed that ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know. Ask it how to return that backpack, and it may send the customer to a returns page, an account screen, and a return label that the store has never had. That's still a hallucination: an answer that sounds right, comes with total confidence, and isn't true.

Whatever you're building, the fix is the same: stop trusting the model with the parts it can get wrong, and check its work before anyone sees it.

Sources indicate that in this tutorial we'll build a small support bot for a made-up outdoor gear store, three times over. The first version is the prompt plenty of bots start with. Then we'll apply five fixes, run six tricky customer emails through every version, and finish with a bot where the model can't slip a made-up price, date, or product past the code.

In a recent development, an LLM hallucination is output that's fluent and confident but not backed by the facts: a product that doesn't exist, a policy nobody wrote, a date that's a week out, or a citation to a paper that was never published. The word covers two different failures:.

Each one needs a different fix, so it helps to keep them apart.

According to recent reports, A language model writes by predicting likely text, one token at a time. It has no separate store of facts it checks against, and nothing in that process says "stop, you don't know this". Training adds to the problem. OpenAI's research on why language models hallucinate points out that when models are graded only on how many answers they get right, a guess scores better than "I don't know", so they learn to guess.

A few things make it worse in your app:.

It has been revealed that newer models are much better at the first one. They'll often say they don't know a price rather than invent one. But they still fill gaps with what's typical, and what's typical isn't always what's true for your business. You can't train that out of a model you call through an API. What you can change is what you ask it to do, what you give it, and what you check.

A made-up answer costs more than one bad reply. Some of the costs are already on the record:.

In a support inbox, the cost is quieter but adds up: a refund you didn't owe, or a customer who goes looking for a live chat button that isn't there and doesn't come back.

It has been revealed that northwind Outdoor sells four things: two packs, a rain cover, and a tent. It has two orders on file and three short policies. Here's all of it:.

Six emails come in, and each one is there to trip the bot in a different way:.

The traps: the 40L pack doesn't come in green, but the 28L does. The 40L is water-resistant, not waterproof. There's no 60L. Whether the return is allowed depends on a membership, a sale price, and a count of days since delivery. The tracking details are in one order record. And the store has no price match policy at all.

Make a folder, add "type": "module" to its package.json, and install the Anthropic SDK and Zod:.

Every version calls the model through one small helper:.

We're using Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort. These are short, simple replies, so the model doesn't need to think for long. Swap in any model you like, because none of the fixes depend on it.

Opus 5.5 didn't invent a single price, colour, or delivery date across the six emails. Every reply stated it couldn't see the store's details. That's real progress compared with older models, but look at what it said instead. Here's the reply to the email about a pack the store doesn't sell:.

In a recent development, it treats the Ridgeline 60L as real and offers to help pick a fit. The other replies made up the store around the customer:.

Northwind has none of those. None of it is a wild guess: it's what a typical online store has. That's exactly why it's dangerous. A customer who goes looking for the live chat or the newsletter discount won't find it, and the bot never answered the question anyway.

It has been revealed that the model can't know Northwind's prices, so give them to it. This is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find the records that matter and put them in the prompt. Our store is small enough to send all of it.

Two things changed. The store data goes in the system prompt, wrapped in tags so the model can tell data from instructions. And the prompt tells it to answer only from that data. Here's the green pack email again:.

Right on all three counts, and it even pointed to the pack that does come in green. The return, which needs four facts from two places, came back right as well:.

According to recent reports, delivered October 6, a Trail Club member, so 60 days, so December 5. Bought on sale, so store credit for what was paid, not the list price. Version 2 got all six emails right.

The last line of that prompt matters as much as the data: "If the answer isn't in the data, say you don't know and that a team member will reply by email." Without it, a model that can't find the answer has to choose between letting the customer down and guessing, and training has taught it to guess. With it, "I don't know" is a right answer, not a failure.

The price match email is the test, since the store data notes nothing about price matching:.

It noted it didn't know, passed the question to a person, and answered the parts it could from the data.

If version 2 got everything right, why build a version 3? Because "right on this run" isn't the same as "right every time":.

The next three fixes take the facts and the rules away from the model completely.

Version 3 splits the work into three steps. First, the model reads the email, but instead of writing a reply, it fills in a form. Every field is a choice from a list, a yes or no, or text copied from the email:.

In a recent development, zod describes the form, and z.toJSONSchema() turns it into a JSON schema for the API's structured outputs. The API holds the model to that schema, so product can only be one of our four product IDs, not_sold, or none. There's no way for it to answer ridgeline-60. Zod then checks the answer again, so the rest of the code gets a typed object. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema goes deeper on this pattern.

Here's what it read from the 60L email:.

The model is still reading natural language, which it's very good at. It just isn't trusted to know what the store sells anymore.

Recent findings suggest that A form also makes the model's mistakes easy to see. The first time I ran this, the form had no asks_something_else field, and the model filed the price match email under product. The reply didn't make anything up, but the email never reached a person. In version 2, a mistake like that would be hidden inside a paragraph. Here it was one wrong value in a JSON object, and the fix was one more field.

According to recent reports, if all you need from this step is decisions like these, a model built for typed answers can do it faster and for less. Our typed AI pipeline tutorial builds the same kind of email sorter with Jev and Clairic.

Recent findings suggest that second step: plain code takes the form, looks up the product and the order, applies the rules, and does the maths. What comes out is a list of facts in plain sentences:.

For the return email, that gives:.

It has been revealed that every number in there was worked out by code that does the same thing every time, and that you can unit test. The 34 days, the December 5 deadline, and the $151.20 in store credit come out the same on every run, whatever the model does.

The last rule in decide() matters most. If an email asks something the rules don't cover, the facts say so and the email goes to a person. Code decides when to say "I don't know", not the model.

Third step: the model writes the reply from the facts and nothing else. Writing is the one job here it does better than code.

Even with the right facts, a model writing a reply can still add something: a helpful "ships in 1–2 business days", or a price it remembers from somewhere. So the last step checks the reply. Anything that looks like a number, an order number, or a product name has to appear in the email or the facts:.

In a recent development, it's simple on purpose. It doesn't understand the reply. It just refuses to let through a value that came from nowhere, and that covers the hallucinations that cost money: prices, dates, quantities, and products. Nothing in the reply can talk it out of a result.

The writer runs the check on every draft:.

Industry observers note that if a draft fails, the model gets one retry and is told exactly which values weren't in the facts. If the retry fails too, the customer gets the facts as a plain list. That's less charming, but it's true.

A check like this will raise false alarms, and that's fine. On my first run, it read a line about the tent's 2.1 kg weight as a product called "Weighs 2" and sent the draft back for a retry. The weight was right, and it was the only thing flagged. A false alarm costs a few seconds. A missed one costs a customer. I tightened the patterns (the version above has the fix), but I'd still rather it flag too much than too little.

It's the same thing that separates the better agentic AI coding tools from autocomplete: they run the tests and read the errors instead of trusting their first draft. Model output isn't finished until something other than the model has checked it.

According to recent reports, this script sends each email through all three versions, saves every reply, and runs the check from Fix 5 over all of them. Versions 1 and 2 are checked against everything the store knows:.

Industry observers note that the check caught one thing in version 1: the "1–2 business days" it made up for processing an order. It missed the "up to 24 hours" for tracking in the same reply, but only because $24 is the rain cover's price, so 24 counted as a known number. And it couldn't catch the invented returns page or live chat at all, because they aren't numbers. That's why the check is the last fix, not the only one.

Reading all 18 replies, here's how each version did:.

According to recent reports, version 3 was less helpful than version 2 in one place. It couldn't give the rain cover's price, because decide() only adds facts about the product the email names. Version 2 had the whole store to look at. In version 3, the fix is a rule you write once: when a product has an add-on, include the add-on's facts too.

Here's version 3's reply to the price match email:.

It has been revealed that no model is free of hallucinations, so you can't stop one from ever making something up. What you can do is build so a made-up detail can't reach a customer: let code own the facts, and check the model's output against them before it's used. Where it matters, send anything your rules don't cover to a person.

According to recent reports, it cuts them a lot, because the model no longer has to guess facts it was never given. In our test, putting the store's data in the prompt took the bot from no useful answers to six right ones. It doesn't stop the model misreading what it retrieved, mixing up two records, or filling a gap the retrieved text leaves. Pair it with a way out and a check on the output.

It has been revealed that not really. Temperature controls how random the wording is. A low temperature makes the model give the same answer more often, including the same wrong answer.

Industry observers note that collect inputs that have tripped your app (or are likely to), write down the right answer for each, and run every version of your prompt or pipeline over the same set. Automated checks like the one in this tutorial catch made-up values. Read the replies yourself for the rest, because the made-up returns page above would pass any number check.

Hallucinations come from asking a model to do jobs it isn't built for: knowing facts it was never given, and running small programs in its head. The five fixes take those jobs away:.

According to recent reports, the model still does what it's best at: reading messy text and writing a friendly reply. It just isn't trusted with the facts anymore. From here, try a seventh email that asks two things at once, add the add-on rule to decide(), or extend the check to catch colours and sizes as well as numbers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face transformers library is the standard for working with state-of-the-art models — from experimenting with cutting-edge research to fine-tuning on custom data. Its simplicity, flexibility, and expansive model zoo make it a powerful tool for rapid development.

It has been revealed that but once you're ready to move from notebooks to production, inference performance becomes mission-critical. That’s where SGLang comes in.

Designed for high-throughput, low-latency inference, SGLang now offers seamless integration with transformers as a backend. This means you can pair the flexibility of transformers with the raw performance of SGLang.

Let’s dive into what this integration enables and how you can use it.

SGLang now supports Hugging Face transformers as a backend, letting you run any transformers-compatible model with high-performance inference out of the box.

No native support needed — SGLang automatically falls back to Transformers when needed, or you can set impl="transformers" explicitly.

Let’s walk through a simple text generation example with meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct to compare both approaches.

transformers library is great for experimentation, small-scale tasks and training, but it's not optimized for high-volume or low-latency scenarios.

It has been revealed that SGLang takes a different track, prioritizing efficiency with features like RadixAttention (a memory-efficient attention mechanism). Inference with SGLang is noticeably faster and more resource-efficient, especially under load. Here’s the same task in SGlang using an offline engine:.

Or you can spin a server and send requests:.

Note that SGLang also offers an OpenAI-compatible API, making it a drop-in replacement for external services.

With the newly introduced transformers backend integration, SGLang can now automatically fall back to using transformers models it doesn’t natively support. This means in practice:.

This unlocks faster inference and optimized deployment (e.g enabling RadixAttention) without sacrificing the simplicity and versatility of transformers ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that note that specifying the impl parameter is optional. If the model is not natively supported by SGLang, it switches to transformers implementation on its own.

It has been revealed that any model on the Hugging Face Hub that works with transformers using trust_remote_code=True and properly implements attention is compatible with SGLang. You can find the exact requirements in the official documentation. If your custom model meets these criteria, all you need to do is set trust_remote_code=True when loading it.

It has been revealed that kyutai Team’s Helium isn’t yet natively supported by SGLang. This is where transformers backend shines, enabling optimized inference without waiting for native support.

There are several key areas we are actively working on to enhance this integration:.

Performance Improvements: transformer models presently lag behind the native integration in terms of performance.Our primary objective is to optimize and narrow this gap.

VLM Integration: we are also working toward adding support for Vision-Language Models (VLM) to broaden the range of capabilities and use cases.

It has been revealed that gemma 3n was confirmed as a preview during Google I/O. The on-device community got really excited, because this is a model designed from the ground up to run locally on your hardware. On top of that, it’s natively multimodal, supporting image, text, audio, and video inputs 🤯.

According to recent reports, today, Gemma 3n is finally available on the most used open source libraries. This includes transformers & timm, MLX, llama.cpp (text inputs), transformers.js, ollama, Google AI Edge, and others.

This post promptly goes through practical snippets to demonstrate how to use the model with these libraries, and how easy it is to fine-tune it for other domains.

Here is the Gemma 3n Release Collection.

Industry observers note that two model sizes have been released today, with two variants (base and instruct) each. The model names follow a non-standard nomenclature: they are called gemma-3n-E2B and gemma-3n-E4B. The E preceding the parameter count stands for Effective. Their actual parameter counts are 5B and 8B, respectively, but thanks to improvements in memory efficiency, they manage to only need 2B and 4B in VRAM (GPU memory).

These models, therefore, behave like 2B and 4B in terms of hardware support, but they punch over 2B/4B in terms of quality. The E2B model can run in as little as 2GB of GPU RAM, while E4B can run with just 3GB of GPU RAM.

In addition to the language decoder, Gemma 3n uses an audio encoder and a vision encoder. We highlight their main features below, and describe how they have been added to transformers and timm, as they are the reference for other implementations.

It has been revealed that the easiest way to vibe check the model is with the dedicated Hugging Face Space for the model. You can try out different prompts, with different modalities, here.

Install the latest version of timm (for the vision encoder) and transformers to run inference, or if you want to fine tune it.

The easiest way to start using Gemma 3n is by using the pipeline abstraction in transformers:.

Initialize the model and the processor from the Hub, and write the model_generation function that takes care of processing the prompts and running the inference on the model.

Since the model supports all modalities as inputs, here's a brief code explanation of how you can use them via transformers.

Support for videos is done as a collection of frames of images.

Recent findings suggest that gemma 3n comes with day 0 support for MLX across all 3 modalities. Make sure to upgrade your mlx-vlm installation.

In addition to MLX, Gemma 3n (text only) works out of the box with llama.cpp. Make sure to install llama.cpp/ Ollama from source.

Check out the Installation instruction for llama.cpp here: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/install.md.

Finally, we are also releasing ONNX weights for the gemma-3n-E2B-it model variant, enabling flexible deployment across diverse runtimes and platforms. For JavaScript developers, Gemma3n has been integrated into Transformers.js and is available as of version 3.6.0.

For more information on how to run the model with these libraries, check out the usage section in the model card.

Given the size of the model, it’s pretty convenient to fine-tune it for specific downstream tasks across modalities. To make it easier for you to fine-tune the model, we’ve created a simple notebook that allows you to experiment on a free Google Colab!

We also provide a dedicated notebook for fine-tuning on audio tasks, so you can easily adapt the model to your speech datasets and benchmarks!

According to recent reports, with this release, we also introduce the Hugging Face Gemma Recipes repository. One will find notebooks and scripts to run the models and fine tune them.

Sources indicate that we would love for you to use the Gemma family of models and add more recipes to it! Feel free to open Issues and create Pull Requests to the repository.

It has been revealed that we are always excited to host Google and their Gemma family of models. We hope the community will get together and make the most of these models. Multimodal, small sized, and highly capable, make a great model release!

If you want to discuss the models in more detail, go ahead and start a discussion right below this blog post. We will be more than happy to help!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Nano VL is a state-of-the-art 8B Vision Language Model (VLM) designed for intelligent document processing, offering high accuracy and multimodal understanding. Available on Hugging Face, it excels in extracting and understanding information from complex documents like invoices, receipts, contracts, and more. With its powerful OCR capabilities and efficient performance on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, this model delivers industry-leading accuracy for text and table extraction, as well as chart, diagram, and table parsing. Whether you’re automating financial document processing or improving business intelligence workflows, Llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for fast, scalable deployments.

Check out the tutorial below to start building your own intelligent document processing solutions with Llama Nemotron Nano VL! Owners can also post-train the model further with their own datasets using NVIDIA NeMo.

Recent findings suggest that llama Nemotron Nano VL, the latest addition to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of models, is a vision language model (VLM) designed to push the boundaries of intelligent document processing (IDP) and optical character recognition (OCR). With its high accuracy, low model footprint, and multimodal capabilities, Llama Nemotron Nano VL enables the seamless extraction and understanding of information from complex documents. This includes PDFs, images, tables, charts, formulas, and diagrams, making it an ideal solution for automating document workflows across various industries like finance, healthcare, legal, and government.

According to recent reports, llama Nemotron Nano VL demonstrates exceptional accuracy on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, which tests models on real-world OCR and document understanding tasks. These tasks include text recognition, table extraction, and element parsing across various document types. The model’s advanced capabilities enable it to deliver better performance than current leading VLMs in real-world enterprise scenarios.

Sources indicate that llama Nemotron Nano VL builds upon Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and C-RADIOv2-VLM-H, a Vision Transformer (ViT) that serves as the backbone for visual feature extraction. This allows the model to handle a wide variety of visual elements in documents, including charts, graphs, and other complex visual representations.

Sources indicate that C-RADIOv2-VLM-H Vision Transformer (ViT): The core visual understanding component of the model, C-RADIO allows for high-resolution processing of documents containing complex visual elements. This serves as a vision backbone, excelling across visual domains and enabling the model to process multi-image understanding with high resolution. This technology underpins the model’s ability to handle complex documents containing visual elements such as images, diagrams, charts, and tables.

Industry observers note that C-RADIO is trained on multi-resolution data using multiple distillation techniques. Multiplicative noise was applied to our weights during training to improve generalization.

It has been revealed that llama Nemotron VL further adopts a design that dynamically aggregates encoded patch features, enabling support for high-resolution input without sacrificing spatial continuity. This strategy efficiently processes documents with arbitrary aspect ratios while preserving both local detail and global context. It enables fine-grained analysis of dense visual content—such as small fonts, multi-column layouts, and intricate charts—without compromising computational efficiency or coverage. The model can also preserve the information better and have less distortion, due to the innovation in high-resolution tiling.

By empowering Llama-3.1 8B LLM with this strong vision foundation, Llama Nemotron Nano VL delivers unparalleled accuracy in parsing and interpreting documents.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using several OSS datasets along with data from NVIDIA’s VLM-based OCR solution, NeMo Retriever Parse. This provides capabilities in text and table parsing, along with grounding, enabling the Llama Nemotron Nano VL to perform at an industry-leading level in document understanding tasks. Synthetic table extraction datasets that were used for training this OCR solution were also used for training Llama Nemotron Nano VL 8B VLM to enable more optimal table understanding and extraction.

It has been revealed that llama Nemotron Nano VL excels in tasks like text recognition and visual reasoning, and demonstrates advanced chart and diagram understanding capabilities. Llama Nemotron Nano VL allows for predicting bounding box coordinates in normalized space to enable grounding like tasks and text-referring.

In a recent development, this strong performance is underpinned by high-quality in-domain data combined with a diverse training distribution across document types, languages, and layouts. A robust data strategy ensures coverage across challenging use cases through selective curation, targeted augmentation, and formatting techniques that clarify task intent and reduce ambiguity—resulting in models that generalize effectively to real-world applications.

It has been revealed that llama Nemotron Nano VL undergoes a two-stage training regimen: pre-training followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). The initial pre-training phase focuses on achieving cross-modal alignment between the language and vision domains. This is accomplished through the training of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) connector, which serves as an interface between the two modalities.

For the training process, Llama Nemotron Nano VL leverages a comprehensive and diverse collection of datasets. This aggregated dataset, comprising a total of ~1.5M samples, includes publicly available, synthetically generated, as well as internally curated datasets. A summary of the datasets utilized during the pre-training stage is presented in Figure 1.

Recent findings suggest that in the Supervised Fine-Tuning stage, Llama-Nemotron-Nano-VL is trained end-to-end on a combination of synthetic, public, and internally curated datasets. The data encompasses a wide spectrum of tasks, including but not limited to: OCR, text grounding, table parsing, and general document-based VQA.

The document understanding capabilities of Llama Nemotron Nano VL can be largely attributed to the OCR-focused SFT data blend. Besides simple OCR, many of the datasets involve tasks such as predicting the correct reading order, reconstructing markdown formatting along with semantic classes (such as Captions, Titles, Section headers) and bounding boxes of individual text blocks. The model is also trained to parse mathematical formulas in LaTeX format and to extract tables in LaTeX, HTML, or markdown formats, depending on the prompt.

To ensure robustness across various domains, we apply affine and photometric augmentations to the document images. To improve the table and chart parsing performance further, we enable swapping of tables and charts embedded into the full-page documents between the datasets. This enables the model to handle diverse document layouts and structures.

A large portion of the internally-created datasets are based on Nemo Retriever Parse training data. These include NVPDFTex - a collection of arxiv documents with ground-truth labels consisting of formatted text in reading order, with bounding boxes and semantic classes of text, as well as LaTeX tables and equations; Common Crawl pdfs that are labeled by human annotators; rendered text from Wikipedia with markdown formatting and tables, as well as a number of synthetic datasets targeted at improving table parsing capabilities and dense OCR. In addition, the training blend includes a number of publicly-available datasets, such as DocLayNet, FinTabNet and PubTables-1M, in which we refine the groundtruth labels.

Figure 2 below indicates the task distribution of the training data. As can be seen, a significant portion of the training samples involve OCR along with grounding and table parsing, as well as OCR-adjacent VQA tasks.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using NVIDIA Megatron and utilizes efficient Transformer implementations in NVIDIA Transformer Engine. For multimodal dataloading, we use Megatron Energon. We provide example Megatron training and inference scripts along with hyperparameters and other instructions to enable custom training of VLMs.

Type “a lighthouse on a cliff at dusk, oil painting, warm light” into a text box, wait ten seconds, and a picture that never existed appears. It feels like magic, but it is a well-understood pipeline of language models, neural networks and a great deal of math. Knowing how that pipeline works makes you a better prompter, helps you diagnose bad results, and makes it easier to choose the right tool for a job.

Sources indicate that this guide explains how text-to-image generators turn words into pixels, why they fail in predictable ways, and how to write prompts that work with the model instead of against it. It then compares five tools that consistently produce good results, starting with Pollo AI, and finishes with a practical workflow, a troubleshooting table and an FAQ. Prepares, credits and model versions change often, so confirm current details on each vendor’s site before you commit to a subscription.

It has been revealed that early image generators were mostly GANs, or generative adversarial networks. A GAN pits two networks against each other: a generator that produces images and a discriminator that tries to spot fakes. GANs could produce sharp faces and textures, but they were hard to train, often collapsed into repeating the same few outputs, and were poor at following free-form text.

In a recent development, A second line of research used autoregressive models, which generate an image piece by piece the way a language model generates words. These handled text prompts better but were slow at high resolution.

The shift came with diffusion models. Researchers showed that a network trained to reverse a gradual noising process could generate images with excellent quality and diversity, and that it was far more stable to train than a GAN. Combine that with text conditioning and a compressed image representation, and you get the systems behind most of today’s tools. Newer models increasingly swap the traditional convolutional network for transformers, but the core idea of iterative denoising is still the foundation.

Industry observers note that under the hood, mainstream generators combine three ideas: a way to understand text, a way to represent images compactly, and a way to generate them gradually. The sections below follow a prompt from keystroke to finished picture.

According to recent reports, neural networks cannot read words, so your prompt is first split into tokens, small chunks of text such as whole words or word fragments. A text encoder then converts those tokens into an embedding, a grid of numbers that captures meaning and context. Many systems use encoders trained jointly on images and their captions, so that the text “a red bicycle” and pictures of red bicycles end up close together in the same mathematical space. Some newer systems add a large language model to understand longer, more detailed instructions.

This is why wording matters. The encoder only sees what you wrote, and it has a limited capacity. A short, specific prompt produces a clear signal. A long, rambling one dilutes each instruction.

In a recent development, instead of drawing on a blank canvas, the model begins with random static. The pattern of that static is controlled by a seed number. The same prompt with a different seed gives a different image, because it starts from different noise. If a tool lets you fix the seed, you can make results repeatable and change just one variable at a time.

During training, engineers take millions of real images and add noise to them in small steps until only static remains. The network is then trained to predict the noise that was added at each step, which teaches it to reverse the process. At generation time, the model applies that skill to pure noise, removing a little at each step. Because it has learned what real images look like, the “noise” it removes gradually reveals something that looks plausible.

Industry observers note that your text embedding is fed into the network through a mechanism called cross-attention. At each step, parts of the evolving image can “look at” relevant parts of the prompt and adjust accordingly. A region that will become a lighthouse attends to the word “lighthouse”. A region that will become the sky attends to “dusk”.

A setting called classifier-free guidance, often shown as guidance scale or prompt strength, controls how strongly each step is pulled toward the prompt. The model computes one prediction with the prompt and one without it, then exaggerates the difference. A low value gives the model freedom and often more natural, varied results. A high value follows the words more literally but can produce oversaturated, over-sharpened or distorted images.

It has been revealed that running diffusion directly on full-resolution pixels would be very expensive. The idea behind Stable Diffusion, known as latent diffusion, is to compress images into a much smaller latent representation using an autoencoder. Denoising happens in that compact space, and a decoder turns the final latent back into a full image. This is a major reason high-quality generation now runs in seconds on a cloud GPU instead of minutes.

According to recent reports, the number of denoising steps and the scheduler, which decides how much noise to remove at each step, shape the speed and look of the result. More steps usually add detail up to a point, then give diminishing returns. Many tools hide these settings, but the trade-off is always the same: fewer steps are faster and cheaper, more steps can look more refined.

Most pipelines finish with an upscaler or refinement pass that sharpens detail and fixes small artifacts. Many tools also offer inpainting, which regenerates only a selected region, outpainting, which extends the canvas, and variations, which restart from a related image.

A generator can only produce what it has learned to represent. Models are trained on very large collections of images paired with captions, and the quality, diversity and licensing of that data affect both the output and the legal picture. Models trained on more photographs tend to produce convincing photorealism. Models tuned on illustration and concept art lean toward painterly looks.

This also explains a few behaviors. Common subjects look great because the model has seen thousands of examples. Rare or very specific subjects, such as an unusual machine part or a niche cultural item, often look generic or wrong. Biases in the data can show up as stereotypes, for example in how “a doctor” or “a CEO” is depicted, so it helps to describe the people and setting you actually want.

Pollo AI’s text to image AI is a browser-based generator built around a simple loop: write a prompt, pick a style, generate, and download. Its page highlights HD output and a wide range of looks, from photorealistic scenes to cute cartoons, anime, pencil sketches, isometric art, abstract compositions and surreal visuals. Files can be downloaded as WebP, PNG or JPEG, a practical spread for web work: WebP keeps pages light, PNG preserves clean edges and transparency-friendly graphics, and JPEG works almost everywhere.

Pollo is also part of a wider platform that covers AI video, so a still image you like can become the starting point for motion without switching ecosystems. That matters for teams producing social content, because one workflow can cover both the image and the short clip built from it.

Things to check: the page does not list specific model names or credit amounts, so review the current proposal details before relying on it for high-volume work. Commercial use requires a paid plan.

Best for: quick, versatile image generation across many styles, especially if you also initiative to make video.

Midjourney has built its reputation on strong aesthetics. Images tend to arrive with polished composition, dramatic lighting and a distinctive painterly feel, which is why it is popular for concept art, mood boards, album-style visuals and editorial illustration. It offers style references and personalization, so you can steer results toward a consistent look across a project. It also supports editing and variation tools for refining a chosen image.

Industry observers note that the trade-offs are practical. It is a paid service, and its prompts reward experimentation over literal instruction following, so you sometimes get something beautiful that is not exactly what you described.

Best for: artistic, high-impact visuals where mood matters more than exact specification.

According to recent reports, adobe Firefly focuses on professional workflows and commercial confidence. Adobe describes Firefly’s own models as trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public-domain material, and it attaches Content Credentials metadata that records AI involvement. It connects with tools many teams already use, including Photoshop features like generative fill and generative expand, which suits designers who edit as much as they generate.

Firefly also provides controls such as style and composition references. Its results can feel cleaner and more commercial than Midjourney’s, which is an advantage for marketing assets and a limitation if you want a wild artistic look.

Best for: marketing and design teams that need editing tools and clearer licensing.

It has been revealed that ideogram is known for rendering legible text inside images, a task where many generators struggle. That makes it a strong choice for posters, social graphics, logo concepts, packaging mockups and product visuals that need a headline or short phrase to read correctly. It also offers style controls and a community gallery that doubles as a prompt library.

Even so, long paragraphs of on-image text can still go wrong. Keep the copy to a few words, put it in quotation marks in the prompt, and describe the lettering style.

Best for: graphics that combine imagery with short, readable text.

Sources indicate that leonardo AI is built for creators who want more control. It offers multiple models, fine-tuning options, image-to-image guidance and a canvas for editing, with a particular following among game artists and designers who need consistent characters and assets. Features such as reference-based generation help keep a character recognizable across many scenes.

The wide set of options is powerful but means a steeper learning curve than a one-box generator, and credit systems can take time to understand.

Best for: consistent characters, game and concept assets, and consumers who like tuning settings.

Recent findings suggest that A reliable prompt has five parts. Put the most important part first, because it often carries the most weight.

Compare weak prompts with stronger ones:.

In a recent development, how do text-to-image generators work? They convert your prompt into a numerical representation, then use a diffusion model to remove noise from a random starting image step by step, guided by that representation, until a matching picture appears.

It has been revealed that which text-to-image tool is best? It depends on the job. Pollo AI suits fast, varied generation, Midjourney suits artistic work, Adobe Firefly suits commercial design, Ideogram suits images with text and Leonardo AI suits tuned, consistent assets.

Why does the same prompt give different results? Each run starts from a different random seed. Fixing the seed, where a tool allows it, makes results more repeatable.

In a recent development, can I use AI-generated images commercially? Often yes, but the rules differ by tool and plan. Pollo, for example, notes that commercial use requires a paid plan. Always check the current terms.

Sources indicate that how do I get readable text in an AI image? Use a tool strong at text, keep the wording to a few words, and add the text in a design editor if accuracy is critical.

What file format should I download? WebP for lightweight web pages, PNG for graphics and sharp edges, JPEG for broad compatibility.

According to recent reports, can I turn a generated image into a video? Many platforms support it. Pollo AI, for example, also covers AI video, so you can move from a still to motion in one place.

Text-to-image generators work by turning language into numbers and using those numbers to guide a model that denoises random static into a picture. Once you understand that, prompts stop being guesswork: you give the model a clear subject, style and lighting, you iterate one change at a time, and you fix small flaws locally. Start with a versatile option such as Pollo AI, then add Midjourney, Firefly, Ideogram or Leonardo when a project needs their particular strengths.

According to recent reports, sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training dense embedding, reranker (cross encoder), and sparse embedding models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, paraphrase mining, and more. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a sparse encoder/embedding model and explain why you might want to do so. This results in sparse-encoder/example-inference-free-splade-distilbert-base-uncased-nq, a cheap model that works especially well in hybrid search or retrieve and rerank scenarios.

Sources indicate that finetuning sparse embedding models involves several components: the model, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong sparse embedding models.

In addition to training your own models, you can choose from a wide range of pretrained sparse encoders available on the Hugging Face Hub. To help navigate this growing space, we’ve curated a SPLADE Models collection highlighting some of the most relevant models.We list the most prominent ones along with their benchmark results in Pretrained Models in the documentation.

The broader term "embedding models" refer to models that convert some input, usually text, into a vector representation (embedding) that captures the semantic meaning of the input. Unlike with the raw inputs, you can perform mathematical operations on these embeddings, resulting in similarity scores that can be used for various tasks, such as search, clustering, or classification.

With dense embedding models, i.e. the common variety, the embeddings are typically low-dimensional vectors (e.g., 384, 768, or 1024 dimensions) where most values are non-zero. Sparse embedding models, on the other hand, produce high-dimensional vectors (e.g., 30,000+ dimensions) where most values are zero. Usually, each active dimension (i.e. the dimension with a non-zero value) in a sparse embedding corresponds to a specific token in the model's vocabulary, allowing for interpretability.

Let's have a look at naver/splade-v3, a state-of-the-art sparse embedding model, as an example:.

In a recent development, in this example, the embeddings are 30,522-dimensional vectors, where each dimension corresponds to a token in the model's vocabulary. The decode method returned the top 10 tokens with the highest values in the embedding, allowing us to interpret which tokens contribute most to the embedding.

We can even determine the intersection or overlap between embeddings, very useful for determining why two texts are deemed similar or dissimilar:.

Industry observers note that A key component of neural sparse embedding models is query/document expansion. Unlike traditional lexical methods like BM25, which only match exact tokens, neural sparse models generally automatically expand the original text with semantically related terms:.

For example, in the code output above, the sentence "The weather is lovely today" is expanded to include terms like "beautiful", "cool", "pretty", and "nice" which weren't in the original text. Similarly, "It's so sunny outside!" is expanded to include "weather", "summer", and "sun".

This expansion allows neural sparse models to match semantically related content or synonyms even without exact token matches, handle misspellings, and overcome vocabulary mismatch problems. This is why neural sparse models like SPLADE often outperform traditional lexical search methods while maintaining the efficiency benefits of sparse representations.

It has been revealed that however, expansion has its risks. For example, query expansion for "What is the weather on Tuesday?" will likely also expand to "monday", "wednesday", etc., which may not be desired.

It has been revealed that in short, neural sparse embedding models fall in a valuable niche between traditional lexical methods like BM25 and dense embedding models like Sentence Transformers. They have the following advantages:.

Throughout this blogpost, I'll use "sparse embedding model" and "sparse encoder model" interchangeably.

Sources indicate that the majority of (neural) sparse embedding models employ the aforementioned query/document expansion so that you can match texts with nearly identical meaning, even if they don't share any words. In short, the model has to recognize synonyms so those tokens can be placed in the final embedding.

Most out-of-the-box sparse embedding models will easily recognize that "supermarket", "food", and "market" are useful expansions of a text containing "grocery", but for example:.

whereas we wish for it to expand to "headache", the common word for "cephalalgia". This example expands to many domains, e.g. not recognizing that "Java" is a programming language, that "Audi" makes cars, or that "NVIDIA" is a firm that makes graphics cards.

Through finetuning, the model can learn to focus exclusively on the domain and/or language that matters to you.
