Sprint estimates usually fail because development teams heavily rely on memory and assumptions instead of evidence. They assume similar tasks will take the same amount of time. Based on these half-baked assumptions, most managers plan around ideal sprint working hours. The backlog then fills with commitments that look realistic on paper but often end up delayed.

Industry observers note that actual development rarely follows that plan. There are always unexpected bugs and task dependencies that consume more time than teams account for in their estimates. Even the buffer time set aside for unexpected work may not be enough. This causes tasks to take longer than expected and pushes sprint commitments behind schedule.

According to recent reports, developer time tracking helps teams make better estimates with historical data. It shows how long previous tasks actually took, which provides managers with an evidence-based reference when they are planning similar work.

Reviewing this data before committing to a sprint scope turns estimation from guesswork into an evidence-based process.

Industry observers note that historical time data offers deeper insights, depending on how you collect and analyze it. Most importantly, it explains why planned work took longer than expected.

Before sprint planning, the following records should be reviewed.

According to recent reports, completed task duration: Check the time spent on finished tasks. Managers should compare similar work to understand typical development effort.

Actual versus estimated hours: Management should observe and identify differences between planned and recorded hours. If there are repeated delays, to some extent, it indicates inaccurate estimates.

Carryover work: Review unfinished tasks from previous sprints. Determine whether poor estimates or external delays caused the spillover..

Recent findings suggest that interruptions: Measure time spent on urgent requests and production concerns. These activities reduce the development capacity that you had planned earlier.

Meetings and ceremonies: Review the time being spent on planning sessions and sprint reviews.

Bug-fix time: Examine hours spent resolving defects. You can also compare it to the time for developing new features.

Blocked tasks: Managers should account for the tasks delayed by missing approvals or technical dependencies.

Recent findings suggest that capacity differences: Compare team availability across sprints. Include leave and staffing changes in that time as well.

These records provide the most value when reviewed together. For example, a task may finish three days late even if the development work stayed within its estimated hours. The actual issue could be an external dependency.

Teams should understand these differences before using historical data to estimate future work.

Historical records provide a useful starting point for estimating fresh tasks. However, teams must interpret the data rather than simply copy previous estimates.

The following approaches can improve estimation accuracy.

Sources indicate that the first step is to consider completed tasks that resemble upcoming work. Managers should compare their requirements and technical complexity. Moreover, the development environment should be considered.

For example, suppose a team needs to estimate a new API integration. Three previous integrations required 12, 15, and 18 hours of active work.

The average is 15 hours. This gives developers a reference point for the fresh estimate.

However, the average doesn't tell the entire story. The newly introduced integration may involve unfamiliar authentication methods or more complicated testing.

Review the reasons behind differences in previous task durations. Check whether developers encountered unexpected bugs or unclear requirements.

Industry observers note that as a project manager, I'd consider these details before estimating for the next project. In my experience, they provide more context than an average alone.

Inaccurate estimates can happen; it doesn’t mean that there is a definite planning problem. However, repeated overruns across similar tasks may reveal an underlying matter.

Sources indicate that research suggests the pattern is widespread. A review of software estimation surveys reports that 60–80% of software projects encounter effort overruns, with the average overrun falling between 30% and 40%.

It has been revealed that start by calculating the difference between estimated and actual effort. Here is the formula for it.

Estimation variance (%) = [(Actual hours − Estimated hours) ÷ Estimated hours] × 100.

Industry observers note that suppose a task was estimated at 10 hours but needed 14 hours. The actual effort exceeded the estimate by 40%.

You can compare the results across similar tasks.

In a recent development, for example, database migrations may repeatedly require more time than expected. This means that the team might be overlooking data validation or additional testing. Once the cause is clear, adjust future estimates accordingly.

According to recent reports, avoid increasing every estimate by the same percentage. Different types of work involve different risks. Teams can also break large tasks into smaller parts. This makes hidden development activities easier to identify.

The aim is to correct recurring estimation errors without unnecessarily increasing the entire sprint backlog.

Task duration doesn't always reflect the hours spent developing a feature.

A study of developer workdays by Meyer and colleagues, which tracked 2,197 hours of activity across 20 developers, found that coding accounted for around 21% of the typical day. Collaborative work such as meetings and email took up roughly 24%.

In a recent development, consider a developer who starts a feature on Monday and finishes it on Wednesday. The task took three days to complete. This is pretty straightforward, and the estimation could be based on it; however, the developer may have spent several hours in meetings. Other than that, urgent support requests could also have consumed additional time.

Sources indicate that the actual development effort could be much lower than three full working days. This distinction matters during estimation.

Teams should record focused development time separately from interruptions. They should also track waiting periods caused by blocked tasks. A more appropriate approach would be to use active development hours to estimate similar future work. They should also account for recurring interruptions when calculating sprint capacity.

Industry observers note that for example, a task may regularly wait for security approval. Adding more development hours to its estimate won't resolve that delay.

Instead, the team should recognize the dependency and consider its effect on delivery.

If managers are able to separate these activities, it will help create better estimates without confusing effort with elapsed time.

A precise estimate can create false confidence when a task involves substantial uncertainty.

It has been revealed that suppose similar tasks previously required between 12 and 20 hours. If you estimate the next task at exactly 14 hours, it will overlook notable differences.

Industry observers note that A range of 12–20 hours provides a clearer picture of the possible effort. Developers can then discuss what might push the task toward either end of the range.

For example, the lower estimate can be directly applied to integration, and the upper estimate might be considered for unfamiliar code or additional testing.

Recent findings suggest that in such scenarios, if the requirements stay unclear, consider a short technical investigation before finalizing the estimate. This can help identify dependencies and reduce uncertainty.

According to recent reports, however, estimate ranges should still support practical planning decisions. Teams need to determine how much capacity to reserve for the work.

Choose a planning assumption that reflects the task's risk and available capacity.

As developers learn more about the task, they can refine the estimate.

Historical time data should affect how much work a team accepts during sprint planning. Better estimates offer little value if teams continue making unrealistic commitments.

Reduce Scope After Repeated Overruns.

In a recent development, if several sprints end with unfinished tasks, it is best that you first review why the team missed its commitments in the first place. Once you have identified the causes, use those findings to reduce the next sprint's scope.

In a recent development, teams should prioritize work that supports the sprint goal. Moreover, avoid adding extra tasks just because they appear manageable during planning.

Reserve Capacity for Unplanned Work.

Production incidents and urgent requests can disrupt planned development. To get more reliable estimations, review how much time these activities consumed in previous sprints. Then reserve an appropriate amount of capacity.

Adjust for Complexity and Dependencies.

According to recent reports, historical estimates become less reliable in case unfamiliar technology or additional dependencies are involved. It is best to break complex tasks into smaller components where possible. This helps developers assess the work more accurately.

Nominal capacity represents scheduled working hours, whereas actual capacity reflects the time available after accounting for other commitments.

The Scrum Guide identifies previous performance and upcoming capacity as crucial inputs to sprint forecasting.

When you are selecting backlog items, consider both. Additionally, avoid committing every available hour or deducting the same interruption twice.

In a recent development, historical time data is useful for sprint planning. Most development teams already use project management tools that include basic time tracking features.

According to recent reports, however, these tools don't always break down how developers spend their working hours. For clearer time data, a feature-specific time tracker is more useful because it provides more details about tasks and workloads.

TimeBee is one such developer time tracking tool I've used. It tracks working hours and time spent on projects and tasks. It also provides attendance records and workforce activity reports.

With this data, teams can review how much time previous tasks required. For example, developers can record hours spent building a feature. They can also track debugging and revisions separately. Later, managers can compare these records with the original estimates. This helps them proposal similar work more accurately.

Industry observers note that timeBee also tracks website and application activity. These reports can help teams understand how working hours are distributed.

However, not all activities reflect actual development effort. Sometimes a developer just spends time reviewing documentation or discussing technical problems. Such work may not always appear in TimeBee as active computer use.

In a recent development, apart from that, attendance, leave, and overtime records from TimeBee can help managers calculate sprint capacity. They can review developer availability before deciding how much work to include in the next sprint.

One thing to remember is that developer time tracking should help teams understand workload patterns. It shouldn't be used to monitor every minute of a developer's day. Management should be careful that the aim is to improve estimates and make more realistic sprint commitments.

According to recent reports, sprint retrospectives should include a review of how the planning is going. If you have made a plan, it doesn’t mean you cannot make changes to it. During sprints, keep comparing original estimates with actual task hours. Track your unfinished work for recurring delays.

Industry observers note that ask developers what caused significant differences. Some tasks may have required additional testing. Others may have been delayed by dependencies. Select one specific improvement for the next sprint.

In a recent development, not every estimation difference indicates a planning failure. Unexpected technical challenges are part of software development.

The objective is to improve forecasts over time rather than eliminate every variance.

Sources indicate that historical time data provides a more stable foundation for sprint planning. Developer time tracking helps teams understand what is actually happening within the sprint rather than creating unnecessary pressure for them.

Other than that, the data also reveals how interruptions affect available development hours.

However, time data should guide planning rather than dictate it.

It has been revealed that 1. What is the difference between sprint velocity and time-based capacity planning?

Sprint velocity measures how much work a team has completed during a sprint. It is usually measured in story points. Contrary to this, time-based capacity planning calculates the hours available for planned work. It accounts for meetings and other responsibilities.

Sources indicate that velocity helps predict future delivery based on past performance. Capacity planning demonstrates whether the team has enough time to meet its commitments.

It has been revealed that 2. Which time tracking metrics are most useful for improving Agile sprint forecasts? The most useful metrics include estimated versus actual hours, task completion time, and unplanned work.

According to recent reports, bug-fix time, rework, and blocked tasks also provide valuable insights. Teams should also review available capacity across previous sprints.

It has been revealed that these metrics help sort out recurring delays and estimation errors. They allow teams to forecast workloads more accurately and make realistic sprint commitments.

**3. How can development teams improve estimates when historical time tracking data is incomplete? **.

Sources indicate that teams can start with available task records and completed sprint backlogs. Developer feedback can help fill information gaps. Similar tasks from previous projects may also provide useful estimates.

Sources indicate that when data is limited, teams should use estimate ranges instead of fixed hours. Consistent time tracking in future sprints will gradually provide more reliable planning data.

In a recent development, 4. How can time tracking data help balance workloads across developers during sprint planning?

Time tracking data shows how much time developers spend on assigned tasks and other responsibilities. Managers can review these records to identify uneven workloads. They can then distribute upcoming tasks based on available capacity.

It has been revealed that technical expertise and task complexity should also influence assignments. This helps prevent over commitment and supports a more balanced workload across the development team.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, gradio is an open-source Python package for creating AI-powered web applications.
  • To that end, here are some of the major improvements we've added to Gradio MCP servers as of version 5.38.0.
  • If you've tried to use a remote Gradio MCP server that takes a file as input (image, video, audio), you've probably encountered this error:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gradio is an open-source Python package for creating AI-powered web applications. Gradio is compliant with the MCP server protocol and powers thousands of MCP servers hosted on Hugging Face Spaces. The Gradio team is betting significant on Gradio and Spaces being the best way to build and host AI-powered MCP servers.

To that end, here are some of the major improvements we've added to Gradio MCP servers as of version 5.38.0.

If you've tried to use a remote Gradio MCP server that takes a file as input (image, video, audio), you've probably encountered this error:.

This happens because the Gradio server is hosted on a different machine, meaning any input files must be accessible via a public URL so they can be downloaded remotely.

While many ways exist to host files online, they all add a manual step to your workflow. In the age of LLM agents, shouldn't we expect them to handle this for you?

According to recent reports, gradio now includes a "File Upload" MCP server that agents can use to upload files directly to your Gradio application. If any tools in your Gradio MCP server require file inputs, the connection documentation will now show you how to start the "File Upload" MCP server:.

Learn more about using this server (and important security considerations) in the Gradio Guides.

Depending on the AI task, getting results can take some time. Now, Gradio streams progress notifications to your MCP client, allowing you to monitor the status in real-time!

Sources indicate that as an MCP developer, it's highly recommended to implement your MCP tools to emit these progress statuses. Our guide indicates you how.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to integrate an existing backend API into an LLM, you have to manually map API endpoints to MCP tools. This can be a time-consuming and error prone chore. With this release, Gradio can automate the entire process for you! With a single line of code, you can integrate your business backend into any MCP-compatible LLM.

OpenAPI is a widely adopted standard for describing RESTful APIs in a machine-readable format, typically as a JSON file. Gradio now features the gr.load_openapi function, which creates a Gradio application directly from an OpenAPI schema. You can then launch the app with mcp_server=True to automatically create an MCP server for your API!

Find more details in the Gradio Guides.

According to recent reports, A common pattern in MCP server development is to use authentication headers to call services on behalf of your users. As an MCP server developer, you want to clearly communicate to your users which credentials they need to provide for proper server usage.

Sources indicate that to make this possible, you can now type your MCP server arguments as gr.Header. Gradio will automatically extract that header from the incoming request (if it exists) and pass it to your function. The benefit of using gr.Header is that the MCP connection docs will automatically display the headers you need to supply when connecting to the server!

In the example below, the X-API-Token header is extracted from the incoming request and passed in as the x_api_token argument to make_api_request_on_behalf_of_user.

You can read more about this in the Gradio Guides.

According to recent reports, gradio automatically generates tool descriptions from your function names and docstrings. Now you can customize the tool description even further with the api_description parameter. In this example, the tool description will read "Apply a sepia filter to any image.".

Want us to add a latest MCP-related feature to Gradio? Let us know in the comments of the blog or on GitHub. Also if you've built a cool MCP server or Gradio app let us know in the comments and we'll amplify it!

The Downfall of Jensen Huang — a timeline of allegations and scandals that brought down the king of AI infrastructure

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia rose from a niche gaming hardware firm with an unofficial motto of "Our company is thirty days from going out of business” to becoming the world’s most valuable company by market capitalization in 2024, and co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang was the man behind its meteoric rise.
  • He planned and founded the firm in 1993 alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem while sitting inside a Denny’s diner in the Silicon Valley area.
  • All this came crumbling down for the billionaire founder in a matter of weeks, but the cracks started long before the first accusation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia rose from a niche gaming hardware firm with an unofficial motto of "Our company is thirty days from going out of business” to becoming the world’s most valuable company by market capitalization in 2024, and co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang was the man behind its meteoric rise.

He planned and founded the firm in 1993 alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem while sitting inside a Denny’s diner in the Silicon Valley area. After more than 30 years, Nvidia had thousands of employees, a global footprint, and a name that people equated to AI chips.

All this came crumbling down for the billionaire founder in a matter of weeks, but the cracks started long before the first accusation. Let’s go back and see how it all began. This is an ongoing saga, so we have listed stories related to the scandal below, which we will update as events unfold.

In a recent development, jensen resigned from Nvidia on November 12, after two weeks of news reports accusing him of multiple affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with his own subordinate. This is significant for Nvidia, which has had a single CEO since its inception. Huang was the face of the company, and many of its employees, shareholders, partners, and fans still support him despite the circumstances of his departure. He steered Nvidia into the giant that it is today by having the vision to develop CUDA nearly 20 years before ChatGPT made AI accessible to the average user and buying companies that helped it scale deployments to hundreds of thousands of AI GPUs.

By 2022, ChatGPT’s arrival and subsequent boom set the AI race in motion, with tech giants and AI startups buying up as many GPUs as they could get their hands on. The increased demand for Nvidia’s products caused it to break the trillion-dollar mark in less than a year after the release of OpenAI’s LLM. As the largest individual shareholders of the firm, Huang and his wife, Lori, became some of the wealthiest people in the world.

It has been revealed that the billionaire founder hasn't always gloated about his position. He once stated in a podcast that if he could turn back time, he wouldn’t have founded Nvidia at all, and also cringed at the praises that the Caltech Board of Trustees chairperson heaped on him before he gave the 2024 keynote speech at the institute’s commencement exercises. He has frequently cited his history working as a “Dishwasher, Busboy, Waiter” at Denny’s, noting it under his experience on his LinkedIn page. More than that, people have seen Jensen go where other celebrity CEOs are rarely seen — enjoying street food in Vietnam, dining at a local fried chicken joint in Korea, and even dragging along 35 of Taiwan’s semiconductor CEOs to a restaurant in Taipei.

Recent findings suggest that but even as he’s building his “Man of the People” persona, his position as the head of arguably the most vital chipmaker in the AI industry meant that he was also gaining influence in business and governance. Industry leaders noticed the power that Nvidia held over those who want GPUs to train their AI models, with some of his fellow billionaires begging him over dinner to sell them GPUs. Just weeks into President Donald Trump’s second term, Jensen Huang was meeting with him at the White House, discussing AI policy and hardware export controls — something the Biden administration started in 2022 in an attempt to hold back China’s ambition'sin AI.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Industry observers note that the rivalry between the U.S. and China has been simmering for years, with Chinese companies like Huawei getting blacklisted because of their work with the People’s Liberation Army. In August 2022, about three months before ChatGPT made AI a household term, Washington expanded its trade bans on Beijing and imposed export controls on Nvidia’s H100 and A100 GPUs. The tech giant responded to this by building a new data center GPU that conformed to U.S. standards specifically for the Chinese market, called the A800, by November of that year. Despite delivering only 70% of the performance of the A100 it was based on, the GPU reportedly still saw great demand from Chinese customers.

Sources indicate that however, the A800 only had a relatively short run as the Biden administration once again increased the performance threshold in October 2023, which resulted in the export prohibition of A800 and H800 GPUs to China. This move forced the company to iterate once again, creating new models that it could sell to Chinese companies, like the Nvidia H20. These chips arrived on the market in early 2024, but before the Biden administration ended in January 2025, it proposed even stricter rules called the AI Diffusion Policy. This sorted nations into different tiers based on trust and risk levels — countries in tier 1, which includes the U.S. and its closest allies, have minimal restrictions, while those in tier 3 are effectively barred from receiving advanced AI GPUs containing U.S. technology.

Sources indicate that this is problematic for Nvidia, as China is the second-largest computer market in the world t and represented between 20% and 25% of Nvidia's data center sales. The tech giant lobbied the U.S. government to ease AI GPU export restrictions, with Trump reportedly suspending the proposed Nvidia H20 ban after Jensen spent $1 million to have dinner with the president in early April 2025. The White House went ahead anyway and banned the sale of the AI GPU less than a week after that, resulting in a $5.5 billion write-off for the company.

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang himself had harsh comments about Washington’s trade ban, saying that “export control was a failure,” and that it had caused the organization’s AI GPU market share in China to go from 95% to zero. He even argued that “conceding an entire market the size of China probably does not make a lot of strategic sense, so I think that has already largely backfired.”.

But even as Huang was fighting to have the trade ban on the Nvidia H20 chip lifted, he continued praising Trump’s tariff plan, calling it “utterly visionary.” The president eventually reversed the ban three months later, and by December 2025, he had approved Nvidia H200 exports to China, but only if Nvidia pays a 25% fee. The newer Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips remain out of reach for Chinese companies, though — at least on paper.

It has been revealed that allegations that Chinese companies have been breaking Washington’s trade ban and smuggling Nvidia AI GPUs into China have been circulating since June 2023, after Reuters revealed that vendors in Shenzhen could secure A100 chips when asked discreetly. They reportedly bought these chips from the excess stocks sold in the open market or through intermediaries in India, Taiwan, and Singapore. Another story published in January 2024 asserted that the Chinese military and related institutions, state-run data centers, and even universities continue buying banned A100 and H100 chips. Six months after that, accounts of underground networks dedicated to smuggling AI GPUs — even entire servers — through other countries started emerging.

According to recent reports, in 2025, an investigative report revealed that at least a billion dollars’ worth of Nvidia AI chips were allegedly funneled into China. Some sellers likened the illicit AI GPU trade to a seafood market, with brokers and retailers openly advertising the most advanced Nvidia AI chips online, from RTX 5090 GPUs to complete B200 servers.

Industry observers note that even with all these reports, Huang continued denying that Nvidia’s chips were being smuggled into China. “There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion,” the then-CEO told reporters at Computex 2025. He also added, “The Grace Blackwell system is nearly two tons, and so you’re not going to be shipping — you’re not going to be putting that in your pocket or your backpack anytime soon. And so, these systems are fairly easy to keep track of... but the important thing is that the countries and the companies that we sell to recognize that diversion is not allowed, and everybody would like to continue to buy Nvidia technology, and so they very well monitor themselves very carefully and they’re quite careful about that.”.

Sources indicate that in the midst of all these AI chip smuggling rumors, the Bureau of Industry and Security, the agency in charge of enforcing U.S. trade sanctions, was found to be “inadequate” and underfunded, and it has been relying on outdated manual processes to enforce restrictions on Chinese tech companies. Despite that, companies and individuals across the world are being investigated and arrested for bypassing Washington’s export controls.

Singaporean authorities broke up a smuggling ring in early 2025 that smuggled Nvidia GPUs for Chinese AI lab DeepSeek, resulting in a raid of 22 different locations and the arrest of nine people. In October of the same year, a Singapore tech giant called Megaspeed, which was led by Alice Huang, allegedly diverted $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips. Four Americans were then arrested the following month for shipping 400 Nvidia A100s and attempting to send 50 more Nvidia H200 GPUs to China.

Recent findings suggest that an even bigger smuggling scandal unfolded some four months after the arrests, after three Super Micro employees were arrested for smuggling $2.5 billion of Nvidia hardware into China. The suspects included organization co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, although Super Micro itself was not implicated. The Super Micro case spanned the globe, with Taiwanese authorities raiding 12 locations related to the case in May 2026, with another nine sites and six people investigated in June. Jensen Huang urged the company to fix its export control compliance after the arrests and raids, telling the media, “We insist our partners are compliant. We hope that they will enhance and improve their regulatory compliance and prevent that from happening in the future.”.

But just five months after he made this statement, one stunning accusation unraveled it all.

On October 29, 2026, The New York Times published a report that Jensen Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spy plot through the executive of a firm who was “close” to him — that executive is Alice Huang. Nvidia denied the accusation. “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” a company spokesperson told Tom's Hardware. “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.".

Sources indicate that but a little over a week later, U.S. intelligence sources claimed that the former Nvidia chief had an affair with the Megaspeed executive. This is the same Megaspeed that has been accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to the tune of $2 billion. By the evening of Sunday, November 8, Jensen admitted to the affair, although he did not name the third party in his statement.

In a recent development, many government officials would usually turn a blind eye towards a tech executive’s personal life, but the fact that he is the leader of the U.S.’s premier AI chip maker and that he is also close to the president has caught the attention of authorities. This has led to the U.S. Congress asking him to a closed-door meeting to discuss Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and the FBI investigating his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy.

The admission and allegations led to people digging deeper into Alice Huang. An investigation by The Information revealed that she was connected to a “labyrinth” of companies spanning Singapore, China, and the British Virgin Islands, and that she allegedly helped move around $7.5 billion worth of AI GPU imports. $2 billion was routed from Megaspeed to Speedmatrix, its Malaysia subsidiary, while another $4.6 billion moved directly from the Singaporean company into Shanghai Century Litong, a China-based cloud services company. It has also reportedly bought Nvidia GPUs from other sources, resulting in the estimated total value of its imports.

People close to her also said that she would leverage her relationship with Jensen to customers, often posting pictures with him on her WeChat account, showing potential clients unpublished photos with the Nvidia chief, and even boasting that he would take her to dinner and give her gifts on her birthday. It also seems that Alice Huang was not acting alone. Multiple sources say that Kang Wei, Alice Huang’s husband, was central to the operation to acquire AI GPUs. He even seemingly acknowledged her relationship with Jensen Huang and has jokingly said that she was a personal assistant to the billionaire.

Industry observers note that however, it seems that the straw that broke the camel’s back was another allegation that Jensen had an affair with another woman — this time, with Kimberly Powell, the tech giant’s vice president of health care who directly reported to him. Hours after this revelation, the company board announced that Jensen had resigned from all his leadership positions at Nvidia, with employees saying he looked “broken and shattered” as he left the company he spent over three decades building in disgrace. Nvidia is looking for internal and external CEO candidates. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim chief executive.

It may be the end of an era, but this does not necessarily spell the end for Jensen Huang. Despite his sudden downfall and quick removal from Nvidia, his status as the king of AI infrastructure remains valuable to the AI industry. Elon Musk even noted on X that it “would be an honor” to hire him, and this could ring true for any business that wants to break into the semiconductor space. But does he even want to return?Huang's first public statement after his resignation came on X on Nov. 17, in which the former CEO said he has "outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," and that if asked by the company's board, he would be "honored" to take the job.".

Over 190,000 shareholders, partners, current and former employees, and fans, including Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, have signed an online petition to bring him back as the leader of the company. President Donald Trump called for his reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.The board, however, may not see things the same way. Multiple reports suggest that the board isn't considering bringing Huang back, and instead is focusing on a new candidate, the ongoing investigation into Huang, and preparing for national security investigations.

#34799. Back to The Future: Evaluating AI Agents on Predicting Future Events

📅 17 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1892 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Back to The Future: Evaluating AI Agents on Predicting Future Events

📅 17 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most current AI benchmarks focus on answering questions about the past, either by testing models on existing knowledge (in a static manner, such as HLE or GPQA, or augmented, like BrowseComp or GAIA) or previously solved problems (like PaperBench, DABStep, or most coding evaluations).
  • According to recent reports, forecasting future events is a complex and holistic task: it requires sophisticated reasoning, synthesis, weighing probabilities and genuine understanding, rather than pattern matching against or searching existing information.
  • In a recent development, beyond its inherent importance, this forecasting-based approach also solves many methodological problems faced by current evaluations and benchmarks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most current AI benchmarks focus on answering questions about the past, either by testing models on existing knowledge (in a static manner, such as HLE or GPQA, or augmented, like BrowseComp or GAIA) or previously solved problems (like PaperBench, DABStep, or most coding evaluations). However, we believe that more valuable AI, and ultimately AGI, will be distinguished by its ability to use this past to forecast interesting aspects of the future, rather than merely reciting old facts.

According to recent reports, forecasting future events is a complex and holistic task: it requires sophisticated reasoning, synthesis, weighing probabilities and genuine understanding, rather than pattern matching against or searching existing information. Evaluating models on their ability to predict future outcomes, whether in science, economics, geopolitics, or technology tests the kind of intelligence that creates real-world value.

In a recent development, beyond its inherent importance, this forecasting-based approach also solves many methodological problems faced by current evaluations and benchmarks. Traditional benchmarks that measure accuracy on fixed test sets are inevitably affected by possible data contamination, and without access to the full reproducible training pipeline of a model, it's hard to trust the results. The most serious evaluation efforts now keep their test sets completely private, creating a frustrating arms race between evaluators and potential "gaming the leaderboard" mechanics (Singh et al., 2025).

It has been revealed that forecasting makes contamination impossible by design, as you can't train on data that doesn't yet exist! This creates a level playing field where success depends on reasoning capability rather than memorization.

Perhaps most importantly, predictions about the future are inherently verifiable. We can wait and see who was right, creating an objective, time-stamped measure of model performance.

Recent findings suggest that we therefore propose evaluating agents on their ability to predict future events (Ye et al., 2024; Karger et al., 2025). FutureBench draws from real-world prediction markets and emerging news to create interesting prediction tasks grounded in actual future outcomes. We collect events from platforms and live news coverages and manifold markets, filtering them to focus on emerging events worth predicting. Using an agent-based approach, we curate scenarios that require genuine reasoning rather than simple pattern matching. Think geopolitical developments, market movements, or technology adoption trends - events where informed analysis actually matters.

It has been revealed that this is the obvious question, and it's at the heart of what makes this benchmark interesting! We believe the answer cannot be a simple “yes” or a “no”, as it mostly depends on the actual questions; there are always important caveats to consider. Humans constantly use their ability to weigh current information to predict future events. Aren't most career moves, relationship choices, or even business strategies essentially bets on future outcomes?

It has been revealed that some predictions involve irreducible uncertainty (Will it rain on December 17th, 2027 at noon?), but many don't. When a skilled analyst predicts a company's quarterly earnings or a policy expert forecasts election outcomes, they're using available information to make informed decisions. This is precisely what we're asking AI agents to do with FutureBench! The task isn't to get agents to fortune-tell, but rather to synthesize information and reason under stronger uncertainty than most other benchmarks.

Sources indicate that the agent's prediction quality directly reflects its ability to search relevant information, synthesize complex data, and reason about cause-and-effect relationships. These are precisely the capabilities we want to measure in real-world applications.

It has been revealed that tools like DeepResearch are already used for market analysis and strategic planning. The quality of information collection strongly correlates with decision-making effectiveness. FutureBench is inspired by this evaluation process and tries to compute agents’ quality with objective, verifiable outcomes.

Building a benchmark that tests real prediction capabilities requires a steady stream of meaningful questions. We've developed two complementary approaches that capture different types of future events:.

According to recent reports, our first approach uses AI to mine current events for prediction opportunities. We deploy a smolagents-based agent to scrape a few major news websites, analyze front-page articles, and generate prediction questions about their likely outcomes. The agent reads through and identifies interesting articles and formulates specific, time-bound questions from their content, for example "Will the Federal Reserve cut interest rates by at least 0.25% by July 1st, 2025?".

We guide this process with carefully crafted prompts that specify what makes a good prediction question—events that are meaningful, verifiable, and uncertain extraction time.

According to recent reports, the agent typically generates 5 questions per scraping session, with a time horizon of a single week, meaning that we assume we’ll know the answer to the question after seven days. This gives us a natural pipeline of fresh evaluation material tied to real-world events.

Our second source draws from Polymarket. These questions come from a prediction market platform where real participants make forecasts about future events. We currently ingest around 8 questions per week.

According to recent reports, however, the raw data needs filtering. We apply strong filtering to remove general questions regarding temperature and some questions regarding the stock and crypto markets, which would otherwise be too numerous for practical use in our benchmark. In addition to this, polymarket questions have less constraints regarding the final “realization” time, the actual outcome of the event could be available only next month or by the end of the year. These are still very relevant questions, but the data collection of the outcome is more sparse.

Here's an example of what comes out of our question generation pipeline:.

It has been revealed that the next question is, what does this type of benchmark allow us to measure? The framework operates on three distinct levels, allowing us to isolate exactly what we're measuring:.

According to recent reports, level 1: Framework Comparison Keep the underlying LLMs and tools constant while varying frameworks. How does a LangChain-based agent compare to one built with CrewAI when both use GPT-4 and the same search tools? This isolates the impact of different agentic frameworks.

Level 2: Tool Performance Fix the LLM and framework while comparing different implementations. Which search tool (for example Tavily, Google, Bing) leads to better predictions than other search engines, holding everything else constant? This reveals which tools actually provide value. How much value do tools bring in general with respect to models without tools?

Level 3: Model Capabilities Hold the framework and tools constant while testing different LLMs. Given access to the same set of tools, does DeepSeek-V3 use them as effectively as GPT-4? This measures pure reasoning ability. This systematic approach lets us understand exactly where performance gains and losses occur in the agent pipeline.

According to recent reports, the benchmark also serves as a robust test of instruction following. Agents must respect specific formatting requirements and generate actions that can be correctly parsed and executed. In practice, this often reveals where smaller language models struggle with complex multi-step reasoning.

According to recent reports, 🚀 Try it yourself! Explore the live leaderboard: FutureBench Interactive Leaderboard.

We use SmolAgents as a baseline agent framework for all the questions. We also compute performance on the base models. For the prediction task itself, the agents get access to a focused toolkit:.

This intentionally lean setup forces agents to be strategic about information gathering while still providing the tools needed for informed predictions.

Industry observers note that we compare different models using smolagents as a baseline (you can find the leaderboard on our HF Space). We also run the standard language models without internet access to estimate a general prior. As expected, we see agentic models performing better than simple language models; stronger models show more stable prediction quality. Overall we also find interesting patterns in how different models try to approach a question:.

Recent findings suggest that running this benchmark has revealed insights into how different models approach information gathering. One striking difference is with respect to scraping. GPT-4.1 appears to rely more on search results. Claude3.7 and 4 explore the web space in more detail and tend to use web scraping more frequently; this thorough approach also means collecting many more input tokens during the research process, thus increasing the cost.

Models show interesting approaches to making predictions, for example, to answer the question "Will annual inflation increase by 2.6 or more in June?":.

The DeepSeekV3 agent analyzed June 2025 inflation prospects by searching recent CPI data (finding current inflation at 2.4-2.8%), considered tariff impacts as upward pressure, and concluded inflation would exceed the 2.6% threshold.

Claude3.7 analyzed June 2025 inflation through comprehensive research (11 searches vs DeepSeekV3's 3), systematically gathering May 2025 CPI data (2.4% year-over-year), identifying decelerating monthly trends (0.2%→0.1%), weighing tariff pressures against Fed restrictive policy, calculating precise 0.2% gap needed, and concluded recent deceleration made reaching 2.6% threshold unlikely, answering "No.".

GPT4.1 analyzed June 2025 inflation through targeted searches for market consensus and forecasts, identified May 2025 CPI at 2.4% (below 2.5% expectations), noted weak 0.1% monthly increases, found no forecaster predictions of 2.6%+ for June, and concluded the jump from 2.4% to 2.6% was unlikely given recent below-expectation trends.

Interestingly, Claude was the only model that tried to access the Bureau of Labor Statistics website to scrape it directly, which failed because it is a .gov website and we do not allow this type of action.

In a recent development, the models exhibit distinct reasoning patterns in their outputs. GPT's analysis focused on consensus forecasts as the key signal for future events rather than extrapolating from current data, while Claude's approach exhibited rigorous analytical structure with its systematic pro/con framework and quantitative gap analysis, and DeepSeekV3's output displayed explicit acknowledgment of data limitations and systematic methodology adjustments when initial approaches encountered constraints.

Sources indicate that these behavioral differences reveal interesting patterns in how different models approach information gathering. The variations in web usage and token consumption suggest that models have distinct strategies for tackling prediction tasks, which FutureBench can help us measure and understand.

One challenge is that evaluation can be expensive due to the large number of input tokens. For example, Claude tends to visit web pages frequently, thus accumulating many input tokens. In a multi-turn loop, this can make the number of input tokens skyrocket very quickly. This increases the cost of any subsequent generation, even though most tokens are eventually cached.

FutureBench is an evolving benchmark, as we discover latest findings and better patterns, we’ll keep incorporating them. We would love feedback from the community to understand how to better source questions, which experiments to run and which data is the most interesting to analyze.

Industry News: Consilium: When Multiple LLMs Collaborate

📅 17 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture this: four AI experts sitting around a poker table, debating your toughest decisions in real-time.
  • In a recent development, the platform works both as a visual Gradio interface and as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that integrates directly with applications like Cline (Claude Desktop had concerns as the timeout could not be adjusted).
  • It has been revealed that this wasn't my original hackathon idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture this: four AI experts sitting around a poker table, debating your toughest decisions in real-time. That's exactly what Consilium, the multi-LLM platform I built during the Gradio Agents & MCP Hackathon, does. It lets AI models discuss complex questions and reach consensus through structured debate.

In a recent development, the platform works both as a visual Gradio interface and as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that integrates directly with applications like Cline (Claude Desktop had concerns as the timeout could not be adjusted). The core idea was always about LLMs reaching consensus through discussion; that's where the name Consilium came from. Later, other decision modes like majority voting and ranked choice were added to make the collaboration more sophisticated.

It has been revealed that this wasn't my original hackathon idea. I initially wanted to build a simple MCP server to talk to my projects in RevenueCat. But I reconsidered when I realized a multi-LLM platform where these models discuss questions and return well-reasoned answers would be far more compelling.

According to recent reports, the timing turned out to be perfect. Shortly after the hackathon, Microsoft published their AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), which is essentially an AI doctor panel with different roles like "Dr. Challenger Agent" that iteratively diagnose patients. In their setup with OpenAI o3, they correctly solved 85.5% of medical diagnosis benchmark cases, while practicing physicians achieved only 20% accuracy. This validates exactly what Consilium demonstrates: multiple AI perspectives collaborating can dramatically outperform individual analysis.

Sources indicate that after settling on the concept, I needed something that worked as both an MCP server and an engaging Hugging Face space demo. Initially I considered using the standard Gradio Chat component, but I wanted my submission to stand out. The idea was to seat LLMs around a table in a boardroom with speech bubbles, which should capture the collaborative discussion while also making it visually engaging. As I did not manage to style a standard table nicely so it was actually recognized as a table, I went for a poker-style roundtable. This approach also let me submit to two hackathon tracks by building a custom Gradio component and MCP server.

The custom Gradio component became the heart of the submission; the poker-style roundtable where participants sit and display speech bubbles showing their responses, thinking status, and research activities immediately caught the eye of anyone visiting the space. The component development was remarkably smooth thanks to Gradio's excellent developer experience, though I did encounter one documentation gap around PyPI publishing that led to my first contribution to the Gradio project.

The visual design proved robust throughout the hackathon; after the initial implementation, only features like user-defined avatars and center table text were added, while the core interaction model remained unchanged.

If you are interested in creating your own custom Gradio component you should take a look at Custom Components in 5 minutes and yes the title does not lie; it literally only takes 5 minutes for the basic setup.

The visual roundtable maintains state through a session-based dictionary system where each user gets isolated state storage via user_sessions[session_id]. The core state object tracks participants, messages, currentSpeaker, thinking, and showBubbles arrays that are updated through update_visual_state() callbacks. When models are thinking, speaking, or research is being executed, the engine pushes incremental state updates to the frontend by appending to the messages array and toggling speaker/thinking states, creating the real-time visual flow without complex state machines - just direct JSON state mutations synchronized between backend processing and frontend rendering.

While implementing, I realized there was no real discussion happening between the LLMs because they lacked clear roles. They received the full context of ongoing discussions but didn't know how to engage meaningfully. I introduced distinct roles to create productive debate dynamics, which, after a few tweaks, ended up being like this:.

Industry observers note that this solved the discussion problem but raised a fresh question: how to determine consensus or identify the strongest argument? I implemented a lead analyst system where users select one LLM to synthesize the final result and evaluate whether consensus was reached.

I also wanted consumers to control communication structure. Beyond the default full-context sharing, I added two alternative modes:.

Finally, discussions need endpoints. I implemented configurable rounds (1-5), with testing showing that more rounds increase the likelihood of reaching consensus (though at higher computational cost).

The current model selection includes Mistral Large, DeepSeek-R1, Meta-Llama-3.3-70B, and QwQ-32B. While notable models like Claude Sonnet and OpenAI's o3 are absent, this reflected hackathon credit availability and sponsor award considerations rather than technical limitations.

According to recent reports, for models supporting function calling, I integrated a dedicated research agent that appears as another roundtable participant. Rather than giving models direct web access, this agent approach provides visual clarity about external resource availability and ensures consistent access across all function-calling models.

The research agent accesses five sources: Web Search, Wikipedia, arXiv, GitHub, and SEC EDGAR. I built these tools on an extensible base class architecture for future expansion while focusing on freely embeddable resources.

Since research operations can be time-intensive, the speech bubbles display progress indicators and time estimates to maintain user engagement during longer research tasks.

According to recent reports, after the hackathon, Deborah Dahl introduced me to the Open Floor Protocol, which aligns perfectly with the roundtable approach. This protocol provides standardized JSON message formatting for cross-platform agent communication. Its key differentiator from other agent-to-agent protocols is that all agents maintain constant conversation awareness exactly like sitting at the same table. Another feature I have not seen with other protocols is that the floor manager can dynamically invite and remove agents from the floor and agents.

The protocol's interaction patterns map directly to Consilium's architecture:.

I'm presently integrating Open Floor Protocol support to allow users to add any OFP-compliant agents to their roundtable discussions. You can follow this development at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/azettl/consilium_ofp.

The hackathon introduced me to multi-agent debate research I hadn't previously encountered, including foundational studies like Encouraging Divergent Thinking in Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Debate. The community experience was remarkable; all participants actively supported each other through Discord feedback and collaboration. Seeing my roundtable component integrated into another hackathon project was one of my highlights working on Consilium.

I will continue to work on Consilium and with expanded model selection, Open Floor Protocol integration, and configurable agent roles, the platform could support virtually any multi-agent debate scenario imaginable.

In a recent development, building Consilium reinforced my conviction that AI's future lies not just in more powerful individual models but in systems enabling effective AI collaboration. As specialized smaller language models become more efficient and resource-friendly, I believe roundtables of task-specific SLMs with dedicated research agents may provide compelling alternatives to general-purpose large language models for many use cases.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

According to recent reports, you wrote a good email. You hit send. Then half your list never saw it, because it went straight to spam.

That is a deliverability problem, and it costs more than most teams think. Every email that misses the inbox is a lead you paid for and never reached.

The good part is that deliverability is not luck. Mailbox providers like Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook judge you on a short list of things: who you are, who you send to, and how people react. Fix those and your inbox placement goes up.

This guide covers 10 email deliverability best practices in the order you should fix them, starting with SPF and ending with sender reputation.

Email deliverability is the share of your emails that land in the inbox instead of the spam folder or nowhere at all.

Sources indicate that people often mix it up with delivery rate. They are not the same thing.

You can have a 99% delivery rate and still have most of your emails sitting in spam. That is why your email tool can say "delivered" while your open rate keeps dropping.

The massive mailbox providers stopped treating authentication as optional.

According to recent reports, microsoft followed on May 5, 2025. If you send more than 5,000 emails a day to Outlook.com, Hotmail or Live addresses, you need all three records in place or your mail goes to junk.

In a recent development, send less than 5,000 a day? Follow the rules anyway. The same checks decide inbox placement for small senders too, just without the public warning.

SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a TXT record in your DNS. It lists the servers allowed to send email from your domain.

When your email arrives, the receiving server checks that list. If the sending server is not on it, the email looks suspicious.

A basic SPF record looks like this:.

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) adds a digital signature to each email. The receiving server uses a public key in your DNS to check two things: the email came from you, and nobody changed it on the way.

According to recent reports, your email provider gives you the DKIM record. You paste it into your DNS and switch signing on.

It has been revealed that DKIM also survives forwarding, which SPF does not. If you can only get one of the two perfect, get DKIM right.

In a recent development, DMARC ties SPF and DKIM together. It tells mailbox providers what to do when an email fails both checks, and it sends you reports on who is sending mail under your domain name.

Start with a monitoring policy:.

p=none means "take no action, just send me reports." It is the minimum Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft accept from bulk senders.

In a recent development, don't stop there. Read the reports for a few weeks, fix any real sender that is failing, then move up:.

One more thing: DMARC needs alignment. The domain in your From address has to match the domain used in SPF or DKIM. Plenty of senders have all three records and still fail DMARC because their email tool signs with its own domain.

Recent findings suggest that if you'd rather not handle this in-house, you can also hire a B2B cold email marketing agency such as IntentSignal, Martal or Belkins. A good agency will set up the domains, mailboxes, warm-up and SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for you, and keep an eye on deliverability while the campaigns run.

A newly introduced domain has no history. If it sends 10,000 emails on day one, it looks exactly like a spammer who just bought a domain.

Warm-up means starting small and growing a little each day, so mailbox providers can watch how people react to you.

A simple schedule for a new domain:.

Send to your most active contacts first. Their opens and replies are what build trust early. If bounces or complaints jump, hold at that volume until they settle.

And if you run cold outreach, do it from a separate domain or subdomain. That way a bad campaign can't hurt the domain your invoices and password resets come from.

A bigger list is not a better list. Dead addresses and people who stopped caring pull your numbers down.

Never buy a list. Bought lists are full of spam traps, which are addresses that exist only to catch senders who email people without permission. Hitting a few of them can get your domain blocklisted.

Yes, you lose some sign-ups. What you keep is real people with working inboxes who actually want your emails. That means fewer bounces, fewer complaints and better opens from day one.

It also keeps bots and fake addresses out of your forms, which matters a lot if your sign-up form is public.

In a recent development, most email platforms add these for you. Check that yours does.

These two numbers tell you the most about where you stand.

Industry observers note that the complaint figures come from Gmail's own rules. The bounce figures are the working limits most email platforms use.

A 0.3% complaint rate is only 3 complaints per 1,000 emails. It does not take much to cross that line.

If complaints are climbing, ask three questions:.

Most complaint problems come from one of those three, not from the email itself.

Sources indicate that spam filters got smarter. A single word like "free" won't sink you anymore. Patterns will.

Recent findings suggest that replies help a lot. When someone replies, the mailbox provider sees a real conversation. Ask a question in your welcome email and you'll get some.

Sender reputation is the score mailbox providers give your domain and IP. Everything above feeds into it. A good score means inbox. A bad one means spam, no matter how good the email is.

You can't see the exact score, but these free tools get you close:.

Check them weekly, and right after any big campaign.

A few habits protect your reputation over time:.

In a recent development, aim for 95% or higher inbox placement. Below 90% means something needs fixing, usually authentication or list quality.

According to recent reports, the common causes are missing or broken SPF, DKIM or DMARC records, a high complaint rate, an old list with lots of dead addresses, or a upcoming domain that sent too much too soon. Check authentication first because it is the fastest to fix.

Recent findings suggest that DNS fixes like SPF and DKIM take effect within a day or two. Reputation is slower. Expect two to six weeks of steady, clean sending before inbox placement recovers.

Yes. The 5,000 mark is where Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft start enforcing openly. Small senders are still judged on the same signals, and Gmail asks every sender for at least SPF or DKIM.

Only if you send enough to keep it warm, roughly 100,000 emails a month or more. Below that, a good shared IP from a trusted provider usually performs better.

Industry observers note that sender reputation covers both your IP address and your domain. Domain reputation is the part tied to your domain name, and it follows you even if you switch email providers. Gmail leans on domain reputation more than IP.

If you only have an hour this week, spend it on SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Nothing else works until those pass.

After that, clean your list and keep an eye on complaints. Send emails people asked for, to people who still want them, from a domain that proves who it is. Do that for a few weeks and your emails will land in the inbox again.

Arc Virtual Cell Challenge: A Primer

📅 18 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2251 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arc Institute recently unveiled the Virtual Cell Challenge.
  • Goal Train a model to predict the effect on a cell of silencing a gene using CRISPR.
  • Doing things in the world of atoms is expensive, laborious and error prone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arc Institute recently unveiled the Virtual Cell Challenge. Participants are required to train a model capable of predicting the effect of silencing a gene in a (partially) unseen cell type, a task they term context generalization. For ML engineers with little to no biology background, the jargon and required context can seem quite daunting. To encourage participation, we recapitulate the challenge in a form better suited to engineers from other disciplines.

Goal Train a model to predict the effect on a cell of silencing a gene using CRISPR.

Doing things in the world of atoms is expensive, laborious and error prone. What if we could test thousands of drug candidates without ever touching a petri dish? This is the goal of the virtual cell challenge — a model (most likely a neural network) that can simulate exactly what happens to a cell when we change some parameter. Given that tightening your feedback loop is often the best way to speed up progress, a model capable of doing this accurately would have significant impact.

To train this neural network, we will need data. For the challenge, Arc has curated a dataset of ~300k single-cell RNA sequencing profiles. It may be worthwhile to revisit the Central Dogma before continuing. This essay will build off of this to provide the ~minimum biology knowledge you'll need for the challenge.

The training set consists of a sparse matrix and some associated metadata. More specifically, we have 220k cells, and for each cell we have a transcriptome. This transcriptome is a sparse row vector, where each entry is the raw count of RNA molecules (transcripts) that the corresponding gene (our column) encodes for. Of the 220k cells, ~38k are unperturbed, meaning no gene has been silenced using CRISPR. These control cells are crucial as we will see shortly.

To understand the dataset more concretely, let's select a gene, TMSB4X (the most frequently silenced gene in the dataset) and compare the number of RNA molecules detected for a control cell and a perturbed cell.

We can see that the cell with TMSB4X silenced has a greatly reduced number of transcripts compared with the control cells.

In a recent development, the astute among you may be wondering why you don't just measure the count of the RNA molecules before and after silencing the gene — why do we need the control cells at all? Unfortunately, reading the transcriptome destroys the cell, which is a problem reminiscent of the observer effect.

This inability to measure the cell state before and after introduces many concerns, as we are forced to use a population of basal (a.k.a control, unperturbed) cells as a reference point. The control cells and perturbed cells are not entirely homogeneous even prior to the perturbation. This means that we have to now separate out our true signal, the perturbation, from noise induced by the heterogeneity.

More formally, we can model observed gene expression in perturbed cells as:.

X^p∼T^p(Dbasal)+H(Dbasal)+ε,ε∼Pε \hat{X}_p \sim \hat{T}_p(\mathcal{D}_{\text{basal}}) + H(\mathcal{D}_{\text{basal}}) + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim P_\varepsilon X^p​∼T^p​(Dbasal​)+H(Dbasal​)+ε,ε∼Pε​.

Sources indicate that prior to the Virtual Cell Challenge, Arc released STATE, their own attempt to solve the challenge using a pair of transformer based models. This serves as a strong baseline for participants to start with, so we will explore it in detail.

STATE consists of two models, the State Transition Model (ST) and the State Embedding Model (SE). SE is designed to produce rich semantic embeddings of cells in an effort to improve cross cell type generalization. ST is the "cell simulator", that takes in either a transcriptome of a control cell, or an embedding of a cell produced by SE, along with a one hot encoded vector representing the perturbation of interest, and outputs the perturbed transcriptome.

The State Transition Model is a relatively simple transformer with a Llama backbone that operates upon the following:.

In a recent development, using a covariate matched set of control cells with paired target cells should assist the model in discerning the actual effect of our intended perturbation. Both the control set tensor and the perturbation tensor are fed through independent encoders, which are simply 4 layer MLPs with GELU activations. If working directly in gene expression space (i.e producing a full transcriptome), they pass the output through a learned decoder.

ST is trained using Maximum Mean Discrepancy. Put simply, the model learns to minimize the difference between the two probability distributions.

The State Embedding Model is a BERT-like autoencoder. To understand this more deeply, first we have to take a little detour for some more biological grounding.

It has been revealed that A gene consists of exons (protein coding sections) and introns (non-protein coding sections). DNA is first transcribed into pre-mRNA, as shown above. The cell then performs Alternative Splicing. This is basically "pick and choose exons", cut out all introns. You can think of the gene as an IKEA manual for making a table. One could also construct a 3 legged table, perhaps an odd bookshelf with some effort, by leaving out some parts. These different objects are analogous to protein isoforms, proteins coded for by the same gene.

According to recent reports, with this basic understanding, we can move on to how the SE model works. Remember, our core goal for SE is to create meaningful cell embeddings. To do this, we must first create meaningful gene embeddings.

To produce a single gene embedding, we first obtain the amino acid sequence (e.g SDKPDMAEI\texttt{SDKPDMAEI}SDKPDMAEI... for TMSB4X) of all the different protein isoforms encoded for by the gene in question. We then feed these sequences to ESM2, a 15B parameter Protein Language Model from FAIR. ESM produces an embedding per amino acid, and we mean pool them together to obtain a "transcript" (a.k.a protein isoform) embedding.

Now we have all of these protein isoform embeddings, we then just mean pool those to get the gene embedding. Next, we project these gene embeddings to our model dimension using a learned encoder as follows:.

g~j=SiLU(LayerNorm(gjWg+bg)) \tilde{g}_j = \text{SiLU}(\text{LayerNorm}(g_j \mathbf{W}_g + \mathbf{b}_g)) g~​j​=SiLU(LayerNorm(gj​Wg​+bg​)).

Industry observers note that we've now obtained a gene embedding, but what we really want is a cell embedding. To do this, Arc represents each cell as the top 2048 genes ranked by log fold expression level.

We then construct a "cell sentence" from our 2048 gene embeddings as follows: c~(i)=[zcls,g~1(i),g~2(i),…,g~L(i),zds]∈R(L+2)×h \tilde{\mathbf{c}}^{(i)} = \left[\mathbf{z}_{\text{cls}}, \tilde{\mathbf{g}}_1^{(i)}, \tilde{\mathbf{g}}_2^{(i)}, \ldots, \tilde{\mathbf{g}}_L^{(i)}, \mathbf{z}_{\text{ds}}\right] \in \mathbb{R}^{(L+2) \times h} c~(i)=[zcls​,g~​1(i)​,g~​2(i)​,…,g~​L(i)​,zds​]∈R(L+2)×h.

We add a [CLS]\texttt{[CLS]}[CLS] token and [DS]\texttt{[DS]}[DS] token to our sentence. The [CLS]\texttt{[CLS]}[CLS] token ends up being used as our "cell embedding" (very BERT-like) and the [DS]\texttt{[DS]}[DS] token is used to "disentangle dataset-specific effects". Although the genes are sorted by log fold expression level, Arc further enforces the magnitude of each genes expression by incorporating the transcriptome in a fashion analogous to positional embeddings. Through an odd "soft binning" algorithm and 2 MLPs, they create some "expression encodings" which they then add to each gene embedding. This should modulate the magnitude of each gene embedding by how intensely it is expressed in the transcriptome.

According to recent reports, to train the model, they mask 1280 genes per cell, and the model is tasked with predicting them. The 1280 genes are selected such that they have a wide range of expression intensities. For the graphically inclined, the below demonstrates the construction of the cell sentence.

Industry observers note that understanding how your submission will be evaluated is key to success. The 3 evaluation metrics chosen by Arc are Perturbation Discrimination, Differential Expression and Mean Average Error. Given that Mean Average Error is simple and exactly as it sounds, we will omit it from our analysis.

According to recent reports, perturbation Discrimination intends to evaluate how well your model can uncover relative differences between perturbations. To do this, we compute the Manhattan distances for all the measured perturbed transcriptomes in the test set (the ground truth we are trying to predict, yty_tyt​ and all other perturbed transcriptomes, ypny_p^nypn​) to our predicted transcriptome y^t\hat{y}_ty^​t​. We then rank where the ground truth lands with respect to all transcriptomes as follows:.

rt=∑p≠t1{d(y^t,yp) After, we normalize by the total number of transcriptomes: PDisct=rtT \text{PDisc}_t = \frac{r_t}{T} PDisct​=Trt​​ Where 000 would be a perfect match. The overall score for your predictions is the mean of all $$\text{PDisc}_t$$. This is then normalized to: PDiscNorm=1−2PDisc \text{PDiscNorm} = 1 - 2\text{PDisc} PDiscNorm=1−2PDisc We multiply by 2 as for a random prediction, ~half of the results would be closer and half would be further away. Differential Expression intends to evaluate what fraction of the truly affected genes did you correctly identify as significantly affected. Firstly, for each gene compute a ppp-value using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test with tie correction. We do this for both our predicted perturbation distribution and the ground truth perturbation distribution. Next, we apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, basically some stats to modulate the ppp-values, as with 20,00020,00020,000 genes and a ppp-value threshold of 0.050.050.05, you'd expect 1,0001,0001,000 false positives. We denote our set of predicted differentially expressed genes Gp,predG_{p,pred}Gp,pred​, and the ground truth set of differentially expressed genes Gp,trueG_{p,true}Gp,true​. If the size of our set is less than the ground truth set size, take the intersection of the sets, and divide by the true number of differentially expressed genes as follows: DEp=Gp,pred∩Gp,truenp,true DE_p = \frac{G_{p,pred} \cap G_{p,true}}{n_{p,true}} DEp​=np,true​Gp,pred​∩Gp,true​​ If the size of our set is greater than the ground truth set size, select the subset we predict are most differentially expressed (our "most confident" predictions, denoted G~p,pred\tilde{G}_{p,pred}G~p,pred​), take the intersection with the ground truth set, and then divide by the true number. DEp=G~p,pred∩Gp,truenp,true DE_p = \frac{\tilde{G}_{p,pred} \cap G_{p,true}}{n_{p,true}} DEp​=np,true​G~p,pred​∩Gp,true​​ Do this for all predicted perturbations and take the mean to obtain the final score. If this challenge has piqued your interest, how can one get started? Fortunately, Arc has provided a Colab notebook that walks through the entire process of training their STATE model. Furthermore, STATE will be hitting transformers very soon, so starting with their pretrained models will be as simple as: Best of luck to all participants! This post was originally published here. This is a fantastic primer, especially for engineers coming from outside the bio world. The framing around the challenge of separating true signal from population noise is so well articulated. It reminded me of how easily that complexity translates into real-world healthcare tools, where even basic outcome tracking can be skewed by heterogeneity in patient populations. In this project, openforge.io/mobile-measures-case-study , a PT outcomes platform, we saw how embedding even simple real-time insights into mobile interfaces can transform provider decisions. So it’s exciting to imagine how something like this could evolve into usable tools for clinicians or researchers down the line. We do this for both our predicted perturbation distribution and the ground truth perturbation distribution.

Next, we apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, basically some stats to modulate the ppp-values, as with 20,00020,00020,000 genes and a ppp-value threshold of 0.050.050.05, you'd expect 1,0001,0001,000 false positives. We denote our set of predicted differentially expressed genes Gp,predG_{p,pred}Gp,pred​, and the ground truth set of differentially expressed genes Gp,trueG_{p,true}Gp,true​.

If the size of our set is less than the ground truth set size, take the intersection of the sets, and divide by the true number of differentially expressed genes as follows:.

DEp=Gp,pred∩Gp,truenp,true DE_p = \frac{G_{p,pred} \cap G_{p,true}}{n_{p,true}} DEp​=np,true​Gp,pred​∩Gp,true​​.

If the size of our set is greater than the ground truth set size, select the subset we predict are most differentially expressed (our "most confident" predictions, denoted G~p,pred\tilde{G}_{p,pred}G~p,pred​), take the intersection with the ground truth set, and then divide by the true number.

DEp=G~p,pred∩Gp,truenp,true DE_p = \frac{\tilde{G}_{p,pred} \cap G_{p,true}}{n_{p,true}} DEp​=np,true​G~p,pred​∩Gp,true​​.

Do this for all predicted perturbations and take the mean to obtain the final score.
