📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that loRA adapters provide a great deal of customization for models of all shapes and sizes. When it comes to image generation, they can empower the models with different styles, different characters, and much more. Sometimes, they can also be leveraged to reduce inference latency. Hence, their importance is paramount, particularly when it comes to customizing and fine-tuning models.

In this post, we take the Flux.1-Dev model for text-to-image generation because of its widespread popularity and adoption, and how to optimize its inference speed when using LoRAs (~2.3x). It has over 30k adapters trained with it (as reported on the Hugging Face Hub platform). Therefore, its importance to the community is significant.

Note that even though we demonstrate speedups with Flux, our belief is that our recipe is generic enough to be applied to other models as well.

If you cannot wait to get started with the code, please check out the accompanying code repository.

According to recent reports, when serving LoRAs, it is common to hotswap (swap in and swap out different LoRAs) them. A LoRA changes the base model architecture. Additionally, LoRAs can be different from one another – each one of them could have varying ranks and different layers they target for adaptation. To account for these dynamic properties of LoRAs, we must take necessary steps to ensure the optimizations we apply are robust.

According to recent reports, for example, we can apply torch.compile on a model loaded with a particular LoRA to obtain speedups on inference latency. However, the moment we swap out the LoRA with a different one (with a potentially different configuration), we will run into recompilation issues, causing slowdowns in inference.

One can also fuse the LoRA parameters into the base model parameters, run compilation, and unfuse the LoRA parameters when loading upcoming ones. However, this approach will again encounter the problem of recompilation whenever inference is run, due to potential architecture-level changes.

Industry observers note that our optimization recipe takes into account the above-mentioned situations to be as realistic as possible. Below are the key components of our optimization recipe:.

Industry observers note that note that amongst the above-mentioned, FP8 quantization is lossy but often provides the most formidable speed-memory trade-off. Even though we tested the recipe primarily using NVIDIA GPUs, it should work on AMD GPUs, too.

Sources indicate that in our previous blog posts (post 1 and post 2), we have already discussed the benefits of using the first three components of our optimization recipe. Applying them one by one is just a few lines of code:.

The FA3 processor comes from here.

The problems start surfacing when we try to swap in and swap out LoRAs into a compiled diffusion transformer (pipe.transformer) without triggering recompilation.

Normally, loading and unloading LoRAs will require recompilation, which defeats any speed advantage gained from compilation. Thankfully, there is a way to avoid the need for recompilation. By passing hotswap=True, diffusers will leave the model architecture unchanged and only exchange the weights of the LoRA adapter itself, which does not necessitate recompilation.

(As a reminder, the first call to pipe will be slow as torch.compile is a just-in-time compiler. However, the subsequent calls should be significantly faster.).

This generally allows for swapping LoRAs without recompilation, but there are limitations:.

For more information on hotswapping in Diffusers and its limitations, visit the hotswapping section of the documentation.

The benefits of this workflow become evident when we look at the inference latency without using compilation with hotswapping.

According to recent reports, the optimization recipe we have discussed so far assumes access to a powerful GPU like H100. However, what can we do when we’re limited to using consumer GPUs such as RTX 4090? Let’s find out.

Flux.1-Dev (without any LoRA), using the Bfloat16 data-type, takes ~33GB of memory to run. Depending on the size of the LoRA module, and without using any optimization, this memory footprint can increase even further. Many consumer GPUs like the RTX 4090 only have 24GB. Throughout the rest of this section, we will consider an RTX 4090 machine as our testbed.

First, to enable end-to-end execution of Flux.1-Dev, we can apply CPU offloading wherein components that are not needed to execute the current computation are offloaded to the CPU to free more accelerator memory. Doing so allows us to run the entire pipeline in ~22GB in 35.403 seconds on an RTX 4090. Enabling compilation can reduce the latency down to 31.205 seconds (1.12x speedup). In terms of code, it’s just a few lines:.

Notice that we didn’t apply the FP8 quantization here because it’s not supported with CPU offloading and compilation (supporting issue thread). Therefore, just applying FP8 quantization to the Flux Transformer isn’t enough to mitigate the memory exhaustion problem, either. In this instance, we decided to remove it.

Industry observers note that therefore, to take advantage of the FP8 quantization scheme, we need to find a way to do it without CPU offloading. For Flux.1-Dev, if we additionally apply quantization to the T5 text encoder, we should be able to load and run the complete pipeline in 24GB. Below is a comparison of the results with and without the T5 text encoder being quantized (NF4 quantization from bitsandbytes).

As we can notice in the figure above, quantizing the T5 text encoder doesn’t incur too much of a quality loss. Combining the quantized T5 text encoder and FP8-quantized Flux Transformer with torch.compile gives us somewhat reasonable results – 9.668 seconds from 32.27 seconds (a massive ~3.3x speedup) without a noticeable quality drop.

It is possible to generate images with 24 GB of VRAM even without quantizing the T5 text encoder, but that would have made our generation pipeline slightly more complicated.

Industry observers note that we now have a way to run the entire Flux.1-Dev pipeline with FP8 quantization on an RTX 4090. We can apply the previously established optimization recipe for optimizing LoRA inference on the same hardware. Since FA3 isn’t supported on RTX 4090, we will stick to the following optimization recipe with T5 quantization newly added to the mix:.

In the table below, we show the inference latency numbers with different combinations of the above components applied.

To enable hotswapping without triggering recompilation, two hurdles have to be overcome. First, the LoRA scaling factor has to be converted into torch tensors from floats, which is achieved fairly easily. Second, the shape of the LoRA weights needs to padded to the largest required shape. That way, the data in the weights can be replaced without the need to reassign the whole attribute. This is why the max_rank argument discussed above is crucial. As we pad the values with zeros, the results remain unchanged, although the computation is slowed down a bit depending on how large the padding is.

Since no new LoRA attributes are added, this also requires that each LoRA after the first one can only target the same layers, or a subset of layers, that the first one targets. Thus, choose the order of loading wisely. If LoRAs target disjoint layers, there is the possibility to create a dummy LoRA that targets the union of all target layers.

To see the nitty-gritty of this implementation, visit the hotswap.py file in PEFT.

Industry observers note that this post outlined an optimization recipe for fast LoRA inference with Flux, demonstrating significant speedups. Our approach combines Flash Attention 3, torch.compile, and FP8 quantization while ensuring hotswapping capabilities without recompilation issues. On high-end GPUs like the H100, this optimized setup provides a 2.23x speedup over the baseline.

It has been revealed that for consumer GPUs, specifically the RTX 4090, we tackled memory limitations by introducing T5 text encoder quantization (NF4) and leveraging regional compilation. This comprehensive recipe achieved a substantial 2.04x speedup, making LoRA inference on Flux viable and performant even with limited VRAM. The key insight is that by carefully managing compilation and quantization, the benefits of LoRA can be fully realized across different hardware configurations.

Hopefully, the recipes from this post will inspire you to optimize your LoRA-based use cases, benefitting from speedy inference.

TimeScope: How Long Can Your Video Large Multimodal Model Go?

📅 23 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, timeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos.
  • Recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos.
  • Recent findings suggest that text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, timeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos. By adding short “needle” clips into videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours, it evaluates three skills:.

Recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos. This trend mirrors progress in long-context language models, which excel at reasoning over lengthy text. Following this, vision-language systems now advertise context windows that can handle thousands of frames. But these claims require a closer look: do these models truly demonstrate understanding of the sequence of events? Are they limited to surface-level retrieval \ recognition? It's crucial to ask if their capabilities are being overstated.

Recent findings suggest that text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths. In the video domain, however, we're still playing catch-up. The most common test, Video Needle in a Haystack (VideoNIAH), injects static images as "needles" into videos, effectively measuring visual search rather than true temporal dynamics. As a result, even top-tier models advertising massive frame capacities are rarely trained beyond ~256 frames and see sharp drops on benchmarks like Video-MME when pushed further.

It has been revealed that this measurement gap leaves us wondering: What does it really mean for a model to "understand" long videos? To address this, we're excited to introduce TimeScope, a new open-source benchmark hosted on Hugging Face. TimeScope probes the limits of long-video capabilities by inserting several short (~5-10 second) video clips—our "needles"—into base videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours. With three distinct task types, it evaluates not just retrieval but synthesis, localization, and fine-grained motion analysis, providing a more holistic view of temporal comprehension.

The promise of long-video AI is transformative — enabling agents to summarize hours of footage, detect subtle anomalies, and answer complex questions about extended narratives. Integrated into robotics, these models could analyze prolonged operations, adapt in real time, and push autonomous decision-making. Just as powerful is the vision of a personal assistant that understands daily life and offers continuous, actionable feedback.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, this leads to overstated capabilities. Models might claim to process 10,000+ frames, but training data often caps at 256 frames per clip, leading to degraded performance on longer inputs. We've seen this in evaluations where increasing frame sampling rates tanks accuracy on tasks requiring temporal insight.

TimeScope flips the script by emphasizing three pillars of long-video understanding:.

TimeScope’s key idea is using short video clips as “needles,” and instead of just spotting the needle, it pushes models to deeply understand the whole video. We start with a long base video (e.g., a documentary, lecture, or ambient footage) and insert one or more hand-curated short video needles (5-10 seconds each) at random positions. These needles contain the key information needed to solve the task, forcing models to process the entire input without shortcuts like sparse sampling.

Industry observers note that figure 1: Overview of TimeScope's needle insertion process. A long base video (1 min to 8 hours) serves as the haystack, into which we splice short video needles (~5-10 seconds). Tasks require detecting, synthesizing, or analyzing content from these needles, embedded at varying depths.

We evaluate across three needle types, each targeting a different aspect of long-video comprehension:.

This tests basic retrieval and understanding of a localized event. Questions are put so that sampling a relevant frame from the needle should suffice—like asking about a shorter part in a longer video.

Example:What mode of transportation is shown in the video?

In a recent development, here, we embed multiple text-based needles (e.g., 2-4 short clips displaying "secret words" via on-screen text) at different points in the video. The model must identify all words and report them in chronological order, simulating tasks like extracting timestamps or key facts from dispersed scenes. This requires scanning the full timeline and understanding relative positioning.

For questions focusing on motion or sequences within a short clip, single-frame sampling won't cut it—the model needs to perceive dynamics across frames. This probes whether long-context handling preserves temporal fidelity.

According to recent reports, example:How many times did the man swing his axe? (a) one (b) two (c) three (d) four (e) five (f) six.

With different video lengths and varying needle placements, TimeScope measures how much video a model can really handle—and indicates that performance drops as the video gets longer.

To kick things off, we ran TimeScope on a suite of leading vision-language models, from open-source favorites to the juggernauts like Gemini 2.5-Pro. The results underscore the benchmark’s value: even models that claim to handle long videos well still struggle with real long-video tasks. These findings reveal clear patterns—performance cliffs around certain durations, strengths in static retrieval versus weaknesses in motion analysis—and pave the way for targeted improvements in model training. For detailed results and visualizations, check out our Hugging Face Space embedded above.

Industry observers note that model size isn’t everything. Qwen 2.5-VL 3B and 7B, as well as InternVL 2.5 models at 2B, 4B, and 8B parameters, exhibit nearly indistinguishable long-video curves to their smaller counterparts. All of them plateau at roughly the same context length, showing that simply scaling parameters does not automatically grant a longer temporal horizon.

Gemini 2.5-Pro is in a league of its own. It is the only model that maintains strong accuracy on videos longer than one hour.

Sources indicate that trade-offs across tasks matter. Qwen 2.5-VL shines in the Information-Synthesis (OCR) task—identifying and ordering dispersed text snippets—yet it falls behind on Fine-Grained Temporal Perception, where precise motion counting is required.

TimeScope demonstrates that “hour-long video understanding” is still more slogan than reality. By revealing where even state-of-the-art models stumble on temporal reasoning, information synthesis, and motion perception, the benchmark invites us to rethink how we train and evaluate multimodal systems.

We hope this benchmark helps the community make steady, measurable progress toward models that better understand video over time.

We are open-sourcing all components of TimeScope:.

Breaking: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking

📅 25 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the new Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.
  • It has been revealed that TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.
  • Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that is widely used in the data engineering community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the new Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.

It has been revealed that TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. CDC dramatically reduces data transfer and storage costs by uploading or downloading only the changed data chunks. Enable CDC by passing the use_content_defined_chunking argument:.

Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that is widely used in the data engineering community.

According to recent reports, as of today, Hugging Face hosts nearly 21 PB of datasets, with Parquet files alone accounting for over 4 PB of that storage. Optimizing Parquet storage is therefore a high priority. Hugging Face has introduced a upcoming storage layer called Xet that leverages content-defined chunking to efficiently deduplicate chunks of data reducing storage costs and improving download/upload speeds.

While Xet is format agnostic, Parquet's layout and column-chunk (data page) based compression can produce entirely different byte-level representations for data with minor changes, leading to suboptimal deduplication performance. To address this, the Parquet files should be written in a way that minimizes the byte-level differences between similar data, which is where content-defined chunking (CDC) comes into play.

Let's explore the performance benefits of the upcoming Parquet CDC feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.

For demonstration purposes, we will use a manageable sized subset of OpenOrca dataset.

Since pyarrow>=21.0.0 we can use Hugging Face URIs in the pyarrow functions to directly read and write parquet (and other file formats) files to the Hub using the hf:// URI scheme.

Sources indicate that we can see that the table has been uploaded entirely (total bytes == total transfer) as fresh data because it is not known to the Xet storage layer yet. Now read it back as a pyarrow table:.

Note that all pyarrow functions that accept a file path also accept a Hugging Face URI, like pyarrow datasets, CSV functions, incremental Parquet writer or reading only the parquet metadata:.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of the content-defined chunking feature, we will try out how it performs in case of:.

According to recent reports, while this use case sounds trivial, traditional file systems do not deduplicate files resulting in full re-upload and re-download of the data. In contrast, a system utilizing content-defined chunking can recognize that the file content is identical and avoid unnecessary data transfer.

We can see that no newly introduced data has been uploaded, and the operation was instantaneous. Now let's see what happens if we upload the same file again but to a different repository:.

The upload was instantaneous again since deduplication works across repositories as well. This is a key feature of the Xet storage layer, allowing efficient data sharing and collaboration. You can read more about the details and scaling challenges in the From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub blog post.

First write out the original and changed tables to local parquet files to see their sizes:.

Now upload them to Hugging Face to see how much data is actually transferred:.

According to recent reports, we can see that only the upcoming columns and the new parquet metadata placed in the file's footer were uploaded, while the original data was not transferred again. This is a huge benefit of the Xet storage layer, as it allows us to efficiently add new columns without transferring the entire dataset again.

Same applies to removing columns, as we can see below:.

To have a better understanding of what has been uploaded, we can visualize the differences between the two parquet files using the deduplication estimation tool:.

In a recent development, adding two latest columns mean that we have unseen data pages which must be transferred (highlighted in red), but the rest of the data remains unchanged (highlighted in green), so it is not transferred again. Note the small red area in the footer metadata which almost always changes as we modify the parquet file. The dedup stats show / = where smaller ratios mean higher deduplication performance.

Also visualize the difference after removing a column:.

Since we are removing entire columns we can only see changes in the footer metadata, all the other columns remain unchanged and already existing in the storage layer, so they are not transferred again.

Industry observers note that another common use case is changing the column types in the table e.g. to reduce the storage size or to optimize the data for specific queries. Let's change the question_length column from int64 data type to int32 and see how much data is transferred:.

Again, we can see that only the new column and the updated parquet metadata were uploaded. Now visualize the deduplication heatmap:.

It has been revealed that the first red region indicates the new column that was added, while the second red region indicates the updated metadata in the footer. The rest of the data remains unchanged and is not transferred again.

We are going to append new rows by concatenating another slice of the original dataset to the table.

Now check that only the newly introduced rows are being uploaded since the original data is already known to the Xet storage layer:.

Sources indicate that since each column gets new data, we can see multiple red regions. This is due to the actual parquet file specification where whole columns are laid out after each other (within each row group).

Recent findings suggest that here comes the difficult part as insertions and deletions are shifting the existing rows which lead to different columns chunks or data pages in the parquet nomenclature. Since each data page is compressed separately, even a single row insertion or deletion can lead to a completely different byte-level representation starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

This parquet specific problem cannot be solved by the Xet storage layer alone, the parquet file itself needs to be written in a way that minimizes the data page differences even if there are inserted or deleted rows.

Let's try to use the existing mechanism and see how it performs.

Also visualize both cases to see the differences:.

We can see that the deduplication performance has dropped significantly (higher ratio), and the deduplication heatmaps show that the compressed parquet files are quite different from each other. This is due to the fact that the inserted and deleted rows have shifted the existing rows, leading to different data pages starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

In a recent development, we can solve this problem by writing parquet files with a latest pyarrow feature called content-defined chunking (CDC). This feature ensures that the columns are consistently getting chunked into data pages based on their content, similarly how the Xet storage layer deduplicates data but applied to the logical values of the columns before any serialization or compression happens.

The feature can be enabled by passing use_content_defined_chunking=True to the write_parquet function:.

Pandas also supports the newly introduced feature:.

Let's visualize the deduplication difference before and after using the Parquet CDC feature:.

Looks much better! Since the proof of the pudding is in the eating, let's actually upload the tables using the content-defined chunking parquet feature and see how much data is transferred.

Note that we need to upload the original table first with content-defined chunking enabled:.

The uploaded data is significantly smaller than before, showing much better deduplication performance as highlighted in the heatmaps above.

Vital to note that the same performance benefits apply to downloads using the huggingface_hub.hf_hub_download() and datasets.load_dataset() functions.

There are cases depending on the reader/writer constraints where larger or smaller row-group sizes might be beneficial. The parquet writer implementations use fixed-sized row-groups by default, in the case of pyarrow the default is 1Mi rows. Dataset writers may change to reduce the row-group size in order to improve random access performance or to reduce the memory footprint of the reader application.

Changing the row-group size will shift rows between row-groups, shifting values between data pages, so we have a similar problem as with inserting or deleting rows. Let's compare the deduplication performance between different row-group sizes using the parquet CDC feature:.

Recent findings suggest that datasets are often split into multiple files to improve parallelism and random access. Parquet CDC combined with the Xet storage layer can efficiently deduplicate data across multiple files even if the data is split at different boundaries.

Let's write out the dataset with three different file-level splitting then compare the deduplication performance:.

Even though we uploaded the dataset with three different sharding configurations, the overall upload size would be barely larger than the original dataset size.

So far we've used PyArrow, let’s explore using the same CDC feature with Pandas by downloading, filtering then uploading the dataset with the content-defined chunking feature enabled:.

Sources indicate that since Parquet CDC is applied at the parquet data page level (column chunk level), the deduplication performance depends on the filter's selectivity, or rather the distribution of the changes across the dataset. If most of the data pages are affected, then the deduplication ratio will drop significantly.

More details about the feature can be found at:.

In a recent development, we explored the performance benefits of the fresh Parquet content-defined chunking feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. We demonstrated how it can efficiently deduplicate data in various scenarios making parquet operations faster and more storage-efficient. Comparing to traditional cloud storage solutions, the Xet storage layer with Parquet CDC can significantly reduce data transfer times and costs.

Migrate your Hugging Face repositories from Git LFS to Xet to benefit from this here: https://huggingface.co/join/xet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One criticism that has emerged of Nvidia’s Vera CPU, driven by AMD, is that Nvidia – and, to a lesser degree, Arm with its AGI CPU – couldn’t have developed an “agentic CPU,” as the chip is often characterized in Nvidia’s marketing materials. Ian Finder, the head of Nvidia’s data center CPU business, pushed back on that criticism in a recent conversation with Tom’s Hardware Premium at SC26, calling the notion that Nvidia somehow knew about the agentic wave four years ago when Vera development began "absurd.".

In a recent development, “There's a conviction around the design philosophy of the part, right? Am I going to sit here and tell you that we have this magic crystal ball around the agentic moment? That would be absurd, right?” Finder stated. “But what we do have as a organization, and I think this has been proven out in our track record, is [that] we have design intuition.”.

Industry observers note that instead of specifically designing Vera for agentic workloads, which would be impossible without a way to see several years into the future, Finder characterized the part by its codesign with Nvidia’s accelerators, something that the team has continued to work on since its first Grace data center CPU. Coming from the assumption that data centers and AI workloads are accelerated (and they largely are), Finder says the co-design approach on the CPU can start in a “conceptually simple space, like what kind of CPU do we need to keep the accelerator fed and happy?”.

Recent findings suggest that although conceptually simple, Finder continually looped back to a particular word to describe aspects of Vera and, to a lesser extent, Grace. “Opinionated” is the word he used, which in the broader context of Vera’s design, shows up in two places. Grace, Finder says, introduced an opinionated memory system with Nvidia’s Scalable Coherency Fabric, while Vera extends that memory system while adding an opinionated microarchitecture, Nvidia’s Olympus core.

Recent findings suggest that the picture Finder paints is one of Nvidia starting from scratch in this space, contrasting it with the “legacy constraints” of, presumably, Intel and AMD in particular, who have large pools of customers with specific needs. As we described in our original breakdown of the Olympus architecture in Vera, Nvidia’s goal doesn’t seem to be to steal market share from AMD and Intel, but rather to grab market share in a CPU space that’s vastly accelerating on the back of AI agents.

This “clean sheet of paper” approach, and Nvidia’s codesign, led to some natural assumptions about what the CPU should do. “If we have silicon that needs really, really great single-thread performance, [and] we also need concurrency, then we need to get there with IPC instead of frequency. We need to make sure we have good loaded memory latency. We need to make sure we have a lot of bandwidth, and you start to design something on a clean sheet of paper that's not encumbered by dollar-per-core economics.”.

Although Finder was clear that Vera’s design didn’t explicitly center around the agents we see today, there were early indications of the workload. “To say that four years ago, when we started putting pen to paper on Vera, [that] we absolutely saw the agentic moment, would [not] be... something I would claim, but we were starting to see the beginnings of tool calling and things like that. We certainly knew what we needed from a head node, and we knew the overall shape of this problem.”.

In a recent development, as you can see in our Vera CPU benchmarking, the chip doesn’t excel at every workload. And, from the data you can see in our recent AMD EPYC Venice benchmarking, the AMD camp has reclaimed some top spots in several benchmarks. Finder suggests that the superior memory bandwidth of Vera will play a much bigger role in the agentic future as these systems evolve to take better advantage of the compute available.

A portion of the AI industry is focused on tackling the problem of fully utilizing the GPU, Nvidia included. GPUs shouldn’t sit idle for very long (if at all) with the demand today, and they don’t. The challenge today is spinning up these agent sandboxes swiftly, within milliseconds, so that the CPU isn’t sitting idle, either.

Finder provided an example of using a coding agent. If you’ve used a coding agent before, you’re probably familiar with this process. After prompting, the model will make several small tool calls to read and locate files, passing back to the model in between. These are tiny calls, almost negligible, and the vast majority of the time is spent in the model on the GPU. Then, it may start compiling and testing the project, which is much more bound by the CPU. The GPU, Finder notes, isn't sitting idle during that time. It’s being leveraged for another purpose. Finder suggests “that very same thing is going to happen on the CPU.”.

This “very interesting computer science problem,” as Finder described it, is being investigated by AI startups such as Daytona and E2B to spin up and close down agentic sandboxes in milliseconds. And serving more agents will naturally put pressure on the memory system, which is an area where Vera has an edge. “We built a product that does really, really well without such optimizations, but as a design point that really will lean into them when the industry starts to catch up to this,” Finder said.

Sources indicate that vera is a fascinating chip, regardless of what you think of it and how it’s presented in marketing materials (from Nvidia itself or elsewhere). Although Grace was the starting point internally, Vera has ridden the wave of agentic to become a much bigger player in the world of CPUs, and Nvidia has already unveiled that it will follow up with its Rosa CPU featuring the newly introduced Rigel microarchitecture. Vera is an opinionated CPU indeed, and time will tell if that opinion is correct.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

We are glad to announce a long-awaited quality-of-life improvement: the Hugging Face CLI has been officially renamed from huggingface-cli to hf!

Recent findings suggest that typing huggingface-cli constantly gets old fast. More importantly, the CLI’s command structure became messy as newly introduced features were added over time (upload, download, cache management, repo management, etc.). Renaming the CLI is a chance to reorganize commands into a clearer, more consistent format.

Recent findings suggest that we decided not to reinvent the wheel and instead follow a well-known CLI pattern: hf . This predictable grammar makes the Hugging Face CLI more ergonomic and discoverable, while also setting the stage for upcoming features.

To start playing with the fresh CLI, you’ll need to install the latest huggingface_hub version:.

and reload your terminal session. To test the install completed successfully, run hf version:.

Next, let’s explore the upcoming syntax with hf --help:.

In a recent development, as we can see, commands are grouped by "resource" (hf auth, hf cache, hf repo, etc.). We also surface hf upload and hf downloadat the root level since they’re expected to be the most-used commands.

To dive deeper into any command group, simply append --help:.

If you are used to huggingface-cli, most commands will look familiar. The biggest change affects authentication:.

All auth commands have been grouped together with the existing hf auth switch (to switch between different local profiles) and hf auth list (to list local profiles).

Industry observers note that the legacy huggingface-cli remains active and fully-functional. We’re keeping it around to ease the transition. If you use any command from the legacy CLI, you’ll see a warning that points you to the new CLI equivalent:.

We couldn’t resist shipping our first dedicated command: hf jobs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: Trackio is a latest, open-source, and free experiment tracking Python library that provides a local dashboard and seamless integration with Hugging Face Spaces for easy sharing and collaboration.
  • If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how important it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.
  • Most machine learning researchers use specific experiment tracking libraries to do this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: Trackio is a latest, open-source, and free experiment tracking Python library that provides a local dashboard and seamless integration with Hugging Face Spaces for easy sharing and collaboration. Since trackio is a drop-in replacement for wandb, you can get started with the syntax you already know!

If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how important it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.

Most machine learning researchers use specific experiment tracking libraries to do this. However, these libraries can be paid, require complex setup, or lack the flexibility needed for rapid experimentation and sharing.

At Hugging Face, our science team has started using Trackio for our research projects, and we've found several key advantages over other tracking solutions:.

In a recent development, easy Sharing and Embedding: Trackio makes it incredibly simple to share training progress with colleagues or embed plots directly in blog posts and documentation using iframes. This is especially valuable when you want to showcase specific training curves or metrics without requiring others to set up accounts or navigate complex dashboards.

Standardization and Transparency: Metrics like GPU energy usage are key to track and share with the community so we can have a better idea of the energy demands and environmental impacts of model training. Using Trackio, which directly gets information from the nvidia-smi command, makes it easy to quantify and compare energy usage and to add it to model cards.

Sources indicate that data Accessibility: Unlike some tracking tools that lock your data behind proprietary APIs, Trackio makes it straightforward to extract and analyze the data being recorded. This is crucial for researchers who need to perform custom analysis or integrate training metrics into their research workflows.

It has been revealed that flexibility for Experimentation: Trackio's lightweight design allows us to easily experiment with new tracking features during training runs. For instance, we can decide when to move tensors from GPU to CPU when logging tensors while training, which significantly improves training throughput when you need to track model/intermediate states without impacting performance.

Recent findings suggest that ok then, so what is Trackio and how do you use it? Trackio is an open-source Python library that lets you track any metrics and visualize them using a local Gradio dashboard. You can also sync this dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, which means you can then share the dashboard with other people simply by sharing a URL. Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization.

You can install trackio using pip:.

Industry observers note that trackio is designed to be a drop-in replacement for experiment tracking libraries like wandb. The API is compatible with wandb.init, wandb.log, and wandb.finish, so you can simply import trackio as wandb in your code.

Industry observers note that after logging your experiments, you can launch the dashboard to visualize your results. Run the following command in your terminal:.

You can also specify a project name:.

To sync your local dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, simply pass a space_id to init:.

If you are hosting your dashboard on Spaces, you can simply share the URL or embed it anywhere using an iframe:.

Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization — all for free!

When you sync your Trackio dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, the data is logged to an ephemeral Sqlite database on Spaces. Because this database is reset if your Space restarts, Trackio also converts the Sqlite database to a Parquet dataset and backs it up to a Hugging Face Dataset every 5 minutes. This means you can visualize your logged metrics in a Hugging Face dataset at any time easily:.

Tip: you can set the name of this dataset by passing in a dataset_id to trackio.init().

Trackio integrates natively with Hugging Face libraries like transformers and accelerate, so you can log metrics with minimal setup.

No extra setup needed—just plug it in and start tracking.

Recent findings suggest that trackio is intentionally lightweight and is currently in beta. Some features found in other tracking tools, such as artifact management, or complex visualizations, are not available yet. If you'd like to have these features, please create complications here: https://github.com/gradio-app/trackio/issues.

Given Trackio's lightweight and open-source nature, we'd love to work with the machine learning community to design an experiment tracking product that works for all of us!

It has been revealed that most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

Join the best takes, color-match them, add sound and captions, and add disclosure where a platform requires it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while Ohioans have rejected the building of latest data centers at every turn, they might not have much choice in the future. That's if a newly leaked bill that could allow data centers to be classified as public utilities is allowed to progress. The move would see the list of who can qualify for eminent domain law expanded, moving beyond entities owned or operated by municipal corporations, electric cooperatives, and agencies holding a certificate of public convenience and necessity granted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The bill, leaked to WCPO Cincinnati, would add "and an agency holding a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the power siting board for constructing an electric transmission line and associated facilities or gas pipeline and its associated facilities.".

Legal experts have warned that the change could mean a transmission developer, like a power tech giant, would be able to seize land to be used for a data center or a facility that would power one. The writing has been on the wall for a while, too, after it was discovered in June that the Ohio Business Roundtable trade group recommended that lawmakers change eminent domain law to "extend possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once public use and necessity have been established.”.

It has been revealed that this follows a July 2026 report that the government was able to seize private land for fresh transmission lines needed to power new data centers. The law gives the government the power to take private land without the need for the owner's consent, so long as it is for public use and the owner receives appropriate compensation. The government can also delegate the same land-grabbing power to “private entities or common carriers,” which includes utility companies.

Industry observers note that this is already happening, too. Earlier this year, the largest utility company in Georgia required the removal of 30 residential properties in order to upgrade its grid. Residents claimed that the expansion was to power AI data centers, a fact given more weight by the fact that one such data center was located just a few miles away.

It has been revealed that despite this, eminent domain law can still be used for good. Nashville set out to use the same law to block the building of a 69,220-square-foot single-story data center next to a zoo. Nashville Metro Council approved the use of eminent domain as a way to buy the land from a local developer who planned the $700 million data center buildout.

📚 3LM: A Benchmark for Arabic LLMs in STEM and Code

📅 01 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.
  • Arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains.
  • To address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.

Arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains. Most evaluations to date have focused on general-purpose tasks like summarization, sentiment analysis, or generic question answering. However, scientific reasoning and programming are essential for a broad range of real-world applications, from education to technical problem-solving.

To address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation. 3LM is the first benchmark of its kind, designed specifically to test Arabic models in structured reasoning and formal logic which are domains traditionally underrepresented in Arabic NLP.

3LM is made up of three datasets, each targeting a specific evaluation axis: real-world multiple-choice STEM questions (MCQs), synthetic high-difficulty STEM questions, and translated code generation tasks.

The Native STEM benchmark consists of 865 MCQs extracted from authentic Arabic educational content, including textbooks, worksheets, and exam banks for grades 8 through 12. Questions span five core subjects: Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, and Geography.

Recent findings suggest that each question is annotated with metadata including domain and difficulty (on a 1–10 scale). The data was sourced using a pipeline that combined OCR (including LaTeX math parsing via Pix2Tex), LLM-assisted question-answer extraction, and manual review. This dataset provides a realistic testbed for evaluating factual and conceptual understanding in Arabic models using real educational materials.

To introduce greater challenge and diversity, we created a synthetic subset of 1,744 MCQs using the YourBench pipeline. This component draws from Arabic textbook text, which is chunked, summarized, and used as input to an LLM-driven question generation system. The result is a curated set of questions focused on mid-to-high difficulty reasoning, including conceptual, analytical, and application-based problems.

Synthetic STEM provides an notable counterbalance to native MCQs by probing deeper reasoning skills and minimizing answer bias. All generated questions underwent filtering based on clarity, structure, and content validity, followed by quality assurance via manual review.

Recent findings suggest that the third component of 3LM targets code generation which is a growing area of LLM evaluation. We translated and adapted the widely-used HumanEval+ and MBPP+ benchmarks into Arabic, creating the first code datasets that test Arabic LLMs on natural language prompts for programming.

Industry observers note that we used GPT-4o for prompt translation and validated the results with a backtranslation pipeline, rejecting low-quality samples based on ROUGE-L F1 thresholds (< 0.8). Additional human filtering ensured prompt clarity and correctness. The code and test suites remain unchanged to preserve scoring fidelity. Evaluations use the EvalPlus framework for pass@1 and pass@1+ metrics.

Each dataset in 3LM went through a multi-stage development process to ensure data quality, fairness, and representativeness.

For Native STEM, we collected Arabic PDF sources and applied a dual OCR approach to recover both plain text and math formulas. Questions were extracted using LLM-based chunking and pattern recognition, followed by classification into MCQ format with randomized answer order. Final samples were reviewed by native Arabic speakers with STEM expertise to confirm answer validity and readability.

For Synthetic STEM, the YourBench pipeline was adapted for Arabic input. Source documents after ingestion were first summarized, chunked and then fed to a code-controlled generator for MCQ creation. We filtered out image-dependent or ambiguous content, and only retained questions within target difficulty ranges. The result is a set of clean, high-quality synthetic Arabic MCQs for STEM.

For the Code Benchmarks, our goal was to isolate language understanding while preserving code logic. Prompt translation was handled by GPT-4o with verification via reverse translation. Code and tests were untouched to allow evaluation parity with English versions. The result is a benchmark where Arabic prompts can be evaluated directly with the EvalPlus toolchain.

According to recent reports, we evaluated over 40 LLMs, including Arabic-first, multilingual, and general-purpose base and instruction-tuned models. Evaluation was performed using both multiple-choice accuracy and generative completion metrics.

Recent findings suggest that in the MCQ setting, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct achieved top performance across both native (71.8%) and synthetic (67.0%) STEM subsets. For completion tasks, Gemma-3-27B showed the strongest results with 43.2% accuracy on STEM answers.

Industry observers note that in code generation, GPT-4o demonstrated best-in-class performance on both HumanEval-ar (83.5% pass@1+) and MBPP-ar (63.6% pass@1+). These results highlight strong correlation (~0.97) between Arabic and English pass@1 scores, suggesting language-specific prompt quality has a major influence on model outcomes.

Sources indicate that we also examined robustness under distractor perturbation, revealing that instruction-tuned models are significantly more stable than their base counterparts. Prompt engineering and zero-shot design were also shown to meaningfully affect Arabic STEM performance.

We built the benchmark to be easily reproducible using standard tools:.

All scripts, configs, and evaluation pipelines are available in our GitHub repository, and can be adapted to evaluate any model compatible with HuggingFace Transformers or OpenAI APIs.

All three datasets are open-source and hosted on HuggingFace Datasets:.

If you use 3LM in your research, please cite us:.

You can use it in standard chat LLM mode or switch to deep, chain-of-thought reasoning for agent pipelines—enabling dynamic, context-sensitive workflows.

One of the core strengths of AI-Q is transparency—not just in outputs, but in reasoning traces and intermediate steps. During development, the NVIDIA team leveraged both standard and upcoming metrics, such as:.

The architecture lends itself perfectly to granular, stepwise evaluation and debugging—one of the biggest pain points in agentic pipeline development.

Recent findings suggest that deepResearch Bench evaluates agent stacks using a set of 100+ long-context, real-world research tasks (across science, finance, art, history, software, and more). Unlike traditional QA, tasks require report-length synthesis and complex multi-hop reasoning:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GPT OSS is a hugely anticipated open-weights release by OpenAI, designed for powerful reasoning, agentic tasks, and versatile developer use cases. It comprises two models: a substantial one with 117B parameters (gpt-oss-120b), and a smaller one with 21B parameters (gpt-oss-20b). Both are mixture-of-experts (MoEs) and use a 4-bit quantization scheme (MXFP4), enabling fast inference (thanks to fewer active parameters, see details below) while keeping resource usage low. The large model fits on a single H100 GPU, while the small one runs within 16GB of memory and is perfect for consumer hardware and on-device applications.

To make it even better and more impactful for the community, the models are licensed under the Apache 2.0 license, along with a minimal usage policy:.

It has been revealed that we aim for our tools to be used safely, responsibly, and democratically, while maximizing your control over how you use them. By using gpt-oss, you agree to comply with all applicable law.

Sources indicate that according to OpenAI, this release is a meaningful step in their commitment to the open-source ecosystem, in line with their stated mission to make the benefits of AI broadly accessible. Many use cases rely on private and/or local deployments, and we at Hugging Face are super excited to welcome OpenAI to the community. We believe these will be long-lived, inspiring and impactful models.

Recent findings suggest that openAI GPT OSS models are accessible through Hugging Face’s Inference Providers service, allowing you to send requests to any supported provider using the same JavaScript or Python code. This is the same infrastructure that powers OpenAI’s official demo on gpt-oss.com, and you can use it for your own projects.

Sources indicate that you need to install the latest transformers release (v4.55.1 or later), as well as accelerate and kernels. We also recommend installing triton 3.4 or better, as it unblocks support for mxfp4 quantization on CUDA hardware:.

It has been revealed that the model weights are quantized in mxfp4 format, which was originally available on GPUs of the Hopper or Blackwell families, but now works on previous CUDA architectures (including Ada, Ampere, and Tesla). Installing triton 3.4, together with the kernels library, makes it possible to download optimized mxfp4 kernels on first use, achieving large memory savings. With these components in place, you can run the 20B model on GPUs with 16 GB of RAM. This includes many consumer cards (3090, 4090, 5080) as well as Colab and Kaggle!

If the previous libraries are not installed (or you don’t have a compatible GPU), loading the model will fall back to bfloat16, unpacked from the quantized weights.

The following snippet shows simple inference with the 20B model. As explained, it runs on 16 GB GPUs when using mxfp4, or ~48 GB in bfloat16.

The models use attention sinks, a technique the vLLM team made compatible with Flash Attention 3. We have packaged and integrated their optimized kernel in kernels-community/vllm-flash-attn3. At the time of writing, this super-fast kernel has been tested on Hopper cards with PyTorch 2.7 and 2.8. We expect increased coverage in the coming days. Industry observers note that we recommend you use mxfp4 if your GPU supports it. If you can additionally use Flash Attention 3, then by all means do enable it!

According to recent reports, if your GPU is not compatible with mxfp4, then we recommend you use MegaBlocks MoE kernels for a nice speed bump. To do so, you just need to adjust your inference code like this:.

MegaBlocks optimized MoE kernels require the model to run on bfloat16, so memory consumption will be higher than running on mxfp4. We recommend you use mxfp4 if you can, otherwise opt in to MegaBlocks via use_kernels=True.

MegaBlocks MoE kernel acceleration is already available for OpenAI GPT OSS on AMD Instinct (e.g., MI300-series), enabling better training and inference performance. GPT OSS models are reasoning models: they therefore require a very large generation size (maximum number of latest tokens) for evaluations, as their generation will first contain reasoning, then the actual answer. Using too small a generation size risks interrupting the prediction in the middle of reasoning, which will cause false negatives. The reasoning trace should then be removed from the model answer before computing metrics, to avoid parsing errors, especially with math or instruct evaluations.

Here’s an example on how to evaluate the models with lighteval (you need to install from source).

For the 20B model, this should give you 69.5 (+/-1.9) for IFEval (strict prompt), and 63.3 (+/-8.9) for AIME25 (in pass@1), scores within expected range for a reasoning model of this size.

If you want to do your custom evaluation script, note that to filter out the reasoning tags properly, you will need to use skip_special_tokens=False in the tokenizer, in order to get the full trace in the model output (to filter reasoning using the same string pairs as in the example above) - you can discover why below.

OpenAI GPT OSS uses the concept of “channels” in its outputs. Most of the time, you will see an “analysis” channel that contains things that are not intended to be sent to the end-user, like chains of thought, and a “final” channel containing messages that are actually intended to be displayed to the user.

Assuming no tools are being used, the structure of the model output looks like this:.

Sources indicate that most of the time, you should ignore everything except the text after <|channel|>final<|message|>. Only this text should be appended to the chat as the assistant message, or displayed to the user. There are two exceptions to this rule, though: You may need to include analysis messages in the history during training or if the model is calling external tools.

When training: If you’re formatting examples for training, you generally want to include the chain of thought in the final message. The right place to do this is in the thinking key.

You can feel free to include thinking keys in previous turns, or when you’re doing inference rather than training, but they will generally be ignored. The chat template will only ever include the most recent chain of thought, and only in training (when add_generation_prompt=False and the final turn is an assistant turn).

In a recent development, the reason why we do it this way is subtle: The OpenAI gpt-oss models were trained on multi-turn data where all but the final chain of thought was dropped. This means that when you want to fine-tune an OpenAI gpt-oss model, you should do the same.

Recent findings suggest that openAI GPT OSS is unusual because it distinguishes between a “system” message and a “developer” message at the start of the chat, but most other models only use “system”. In GPT OSS, the system message follows a strict format and contains information like the current date, the model identity and the level of reasoning effort to use, and the “developer” message is more freeform, which makes it (very confusingly) similar to the “system” messages of most other models.

To make GPT OSS easier to use with the standard API, the chat template will treat a message with “system” or “developer” role as the developer message. If you want to modify the actual system message, you can pass the specific arguments model_identity or reasoning_effort to the chat template:.

GPT OSS supports two kinds of tools: The “builtin” tools browser and python, and custom tools supplied by the user. To enable builtin tools, pass their names in a list to the builtin_tools argument of the chat template, as shown below. To pass custom tools, you can pass them either as JSON schema or as Python functions with type hints and docstrings using the tools argument. See the chat template tools documentation for more details, or you can just modify the example below:.

If the model chooses to call a tool (indicated by a message ending in <|call|>), then you should add the tool call to the chat, call the tool, then add the tool result to the chat and generate again:.

This is a genuinely impressive and consequential release. Open-weight models at this scale, with Apache 2.0 licensing and serious attention to inference efficiency, feel like a real inflection point rather than a symbolic gesture. The combination of MoE architecture, MXFP4 quantization, and practical ecosystem support (Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and ROCm) makes this usable today, not just theoretically interesting.

Industry observers note that what stands out most is the emphasis on deployment reality: single-H100 feasibility for 120B, 16GB consumer GPUs for 20B, and first-class support for multiple inference backends. That’s exactly what developers and researchers need if these models are going to be experimented with, fine-tuned, and embedded into real products rather than living only in benchmarks.

It’s also refreshing to see clear guidance around reasoning traces, chat templates, and evaluation pitfalls. Too many “reasoning models” gloss over those operational details, which matter a lot once you leave the demo stage.

Industry observers note that as someone working across text, vision, and creative tooling, I also appreciate how releases like this pair well with the broader AI stack. Strong open reasoning models combined with next-gen creative tools—like Experience the future of AI image editing—open up some very compelling hybrid workflows for agents, content pipelines, and local-first applications.

Sources indicate that overall, this feels like a long-lived contribution to the open ecosystem, not a short-term headline. Kudos to OpenAI and Hugging Face for shipping something that’s both ambitious and genuinely usable.

Recent findings suggest that not long ago, a synthetic voice was easy to spot: flat, rushed and strangely stressed. Today, the best AI text to speech tools can read a script with natural pacing, switch accents, whisper or laugh on cue, and even speak in a voice cloned from a short recording. That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

This guide explains how modern text-to-speech works, what to look for when choosing a tool, and compares six options: OpenArt, ElevenLabs, Murf AI, Speechify, WellSaid Labs and Amazon Polly. Each section covers strengths, limits and the best use case. The details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing, and plans, models and prices change often, so confirm current terms before you commit.

OpenArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

Sources indicate that the direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt says Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

Because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

Pricing: Newly introduced accounts get 40 free credits. Paid prepares add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

Recent findings suggest that elevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

For developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free plan includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid plans start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

In a recent development, pricing: Free plan with 10,000 credits a month. Paid plans from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

It has been revealed that murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

Sources indicate that murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

Industry observers note that pricing: Free strategy with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

Speechify is built around reading aloud. You paste text or upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT or EPUB file, pick a voice, adjust playback speed and listen or download the audio. Its page lists more than 1,000 voices across 60 or more languages, including several regional English accents, and the tool works in the browser and in apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, plus Chrome and Edge extensions.

It has been revealed that the use cases lean toward productivity and accessibility: studying, going through emails and documents, language learning and support for people with visual impairments, dyslexia or ADHD. A free account saves your documents and syncs them across devices.

In a recent development, pricing: You can start free. Paid plans are listed on Speechify’s pricing page.

Best for: students, professionals and anyone who wants to listen to documents and articles.

WellSaid Labs focuses on professional voiceover for businesses. Every voice is built from recordings of a real voice actor who consented and is paid when the voice is used, and the voices are licensed for commercial use. Its page describes hundreds of voices across languages, accents, tones and styles.

Pronunciation control is a highlight. You can highlight a word to see suggested pronunciations and save your choice to a team library that applies to every project, and set pacing, emphasis and pronunciation line by line. WellSaid also describes a Producer product that connects AI assistants to WellSaid through MCP and its API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

Best for: corporate training, product marketing, courses and advertising where licensing and consistency matter.

Industry observers note that amazon Polly is Amazon Web Services’ text to speech service, and it is aimed squarely at developers. According to AWS, it supports more than 40 languages and language variants with over 100 male and female voices, and it works through APIs in your code. It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Sources indicate that pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for fresh accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example shows how little code a basic request takes:.

Sources indicate that the sample uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript, calls the neural engine and sends SSML so that the pause and emphasis are explicit. Adjust the region, voice and engine to match what your account supports.

It has been revealed that pricing: Usage-based with a free tier for new accounts. See the AWS pricing page for current rates.

Best for: apps, IVR systems, notifications and any product that needs automated speech at scale.

In a recent development, treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that says to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:.

The say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

Industry observers note that what is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

Is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free prepares or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for new accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free blueprint, which has no commercial licence.

According to recent reports, can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid prepares, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

Can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

According to recent reports, what is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

It has been revealed that which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

Industry observers note that how do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

It has been revealed that AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that south Korea used emergency disaster alerts during its national college admission test to catch prohibited devices. The anti-cheating measure was announced after a cheater in South Korea’s tax accountant exam confessed to using AI and a micro-camera to cheat. The alerts caught a total of 54 candidates, with 111 total when combined with other means, The Korean Herald reports.

It has been revealed that the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), also known as Suneung, is one of South Korea’s most key yearly events. The exam is so significant that the whole country pauses and makes way for the test-takers; police clear the roads and escort late students, noisy construction and maintenance are suspended, aircraft are grounded, military exercises are paused, and the stock market opens an hour later. The government even requests public institutions and private companies start work later, delaying the rush hour and ensuring the students arrive unimpeded.

The brutal exam, held every third Thursday of November, lasts eight hours, from 8:40 AM to 5:45 PM, often being the deciding factor for the trajectory of the students’ lives. With such high stakes, cheating is not unusual.

The month before the CSAT, South Korea’s Certified Tax Accountant exam received an unusually large number of high scorers — with 66 candidates scoring over 90+ in introductory accounting over only two in 2025 and one in 2024, as reported by The Korean Herald. The top scorer, Han Won-seok, confessed to cheating on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, admitting to cheating using a micro-camera that feeds images of the test to an AI on his smartphone.

The confession went live days before the Suneung, prompting the South Korean government to tighten up its anti-cheating measures for the exam, with Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung stating, "Cheating involving the abuse of AI in South Korea, where public examinations significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources, rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust," calling for an overhaul of the system to address AI-assisted cheating, as reported by Yonhap News Agency.

It has been revealed that the first alert rang at 8:30 AM, ten minutes before the exam started, catching 31 students with unauthorized devices, whose scores were immediately invalidated despite the test not having started yet. The next two alerts at 2:21 and 2:57 PM caught 23 more, bringing the total to 54. As of today, Yonhap News Agency reports that 111 total students were caught with unauthorized devices — 52 were caught through other methods such as metal detectors, WiFi signal detection, and physical inspections, with a further five caught red-handed using prohibited devices.

According to recent reports, alongside the South Korean government’s reaction to the confession, a law school entrance exam candidate accused of AI-assisted cheating like Han Won-seok had died on the day of the Suneung. In July, Lee Jin-woo, a Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET) candidate, achieved an impressive perfect score and is reportedly the first to do so. Months later, he published a book about his study methods, talking about lifestyle changes, exercise, diet, and even reduced smartphone use.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vision Language Models (VLMs) are getting stronger, but aligning them to human preferences still matters. In TRL, we already showed how to post-train VLMs with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). This time, we’re going further.

tl;dr Here’s what’s fresh in TRL:.

These go beyond pairwise DPO, extracting richer signals from preference data and scaling better with modern VLMs.

We’ve also extended existing methods to support VLMs:.

This enables more efficient and scalable multimodal alignment.

Industry observers note that traditionally, you would take a base model, apply SFT to follow instructions, and then apply DPO to align it to preferential data. Previously, we adapted this approach to Vision Language Models (VLMs) and validated it on IDEFICS2, showing improvement in model responses.

DPO works by optimizing preferences between pairs of model responses using a contrastive loss: you have a chosen and a rejected answer and you optimize your preferences based on what you want and don’t want.

But in the last year, latest multimodal alignment methods have gained popularity, GRPO and MPO, that can push VLM performance even further. At the end of the blog post you can find a table that showcases the differences between model responses.

It has been revealed that aligning multimodal models with SFT to do reasoning tasks falls short due to distribution shift. Meanwhile, models aligned with DPO fail to generate coherent rationales and might generate repetitive responses. To address this, there’s a fresh technique called Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO) specifically made for multimodal models. This method is essentially an extension of DPO with multiple losses: preference loss from DPO (sigmoid), quality loss from Binary Classifier Optimization (BCO), and generation loss from SFT. According to the paper, simply switching to this combined loss results in 6.2 pts improvement in MathVista!

Since this is only modifying the loss, we added combined loss support to TRL's DPOTrainer class. To use it, you can initialize the DPOConfig as follows:.

And that’s it! If you want to explore further, you can find a complete notebook example here.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a cutting-edge alignment method initially introduced in DeepSeek Math paper and later integrated to DeepSeek R1, the groundbreaking LLM. It’s an addition to PPO where the policy updates are done over groups (batches of trajectories that represent how a dialogue rolls out). This feature makes it more robust to reward noise, as the noise averages out within groups. Since the model learns broader sense of a good response rather than singular high reward samples, this method also makes the model highly performant.

In TRL, we now introduce GRPO support for vision language models. We will not provide a full training script example, as you can find it in the notebook. Instead, we'll focus on highlighting the key component and concepts.

Recent findings suggest that to make the training script work effectively, we need to validate that the format of the answer is correct and that the solution itself is close to the completed parts, so we write two reward functions. In order to really see improvements in the latter reward, you would need a rather maximalist setup, where you have relatively larger models, a lot of generations, and a high-quality, diverse dataset.

Then, you can initialize GRPOConfig and GRPOTrainer, pass in the reward functions we defined above and call train() to start training.

Explore the full notebook example here.

Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) is a RL alignment algorithm recently released by Qwen that overcomes some limitations of GRPO. It achieves a more stable training computing importance sampling weights at the sequence level instead of per-token. Its benefits are more relevant in MoE style models.
