Verifying formal models of Raft implementations

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Antithesis

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November 19, 2026 | Rohan Padhye, Research fellow | Hillel Wayne, Developer educator.
  • Sources indicate that at Antithesis, we love finding bugs in distributed systems.
  • It has been revealed that in this post, we demonstrate the paradigm on two Raft implementations, production libraries from etcd and HashiCorp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 19, 2026 | Rohan Padhye, Research fellow | Hillel Wayne, Developer educator.

Sources indicate that at Antithesis, we love finding bugs in distributed systems. But Antithesis can also help eliminate certain classes of bugs by using a combination of AI and formal methods to prove the correctness of complex design choices.

It has been revealed that in this post, we demonstrate the paradigm on two Raft implementations, production libraries from etcd and HashiCorp. Although theyâre implementing the same protocol, there are significant differences in the approaches the two use. We used AI, TLA+, and Antithesis to formally model the two libraries with trace validation. We iterated between model checking, Antithesis testing, and proof attempts, each of which exposed bugs in the code or gaps in the model. We patched bugs and refined the model until it was provable, and until every test run was conformant.

Our model handles several extensions to the core Raft algorithm including pre-votes, snapshots, leadership transfers, and, for etcd-raft only: read indexes for linearizability, async storage writes, and membership changes (where etcdâs implementation intentionally deviates from the Raft paper).

The final proofs establish core Raft safety properties such as Election Safety, Leader Completeness, and State-Machine Safety. In other words, our process established that once we applied the workarounds and fixes needed, the specific designs (scoped to the features we modeled) embodied in HashiCorp Raft and etcd-raft actually offer the same guarantees that the Raft paper does. We make the artifacts available for open review:.

Earlier this year, we wrote about how we keep finding bugs in every major Raft implementation we test with Antithesis. This was surprising, because the underlying Raft protocol has been extensively studied, formally specified, and rigorously proven correct (under a set of assumptions). In that post, we pointed out that many implementations subtly deviate from those assumptions, re-design the algorithm for performance, and/or extend the core Raft protocol with unverified extensions â thereby introducing bugs.

Since then, advances in AI have made automated theorem proving and formal verification of complex systems much more scalable, making it feasible to connect a specification to its implementation. So we set out to formally verify not just the core Raft protocol, but the specific designs implemented by production Raft libraries, incorporating custom data structures, different modes of concurrency, and various extensions such as pre-votes, leadership transfers, snapshots, and (in the case of etcd-raft) membership changes.

Recent findings suggest that A key challenge in applying formal methods is to identify a level of abstraction that both allows us to reason mathematically about desired properties, and bridges the gap between specification and implementation. We are not yet at the point of reasoning directly at the level of assembly instructions or even programming language semantics in order to verify distributed safety properties in production systems.

Both Anthropic/Theoremâs OSS-Verify and Google DeepMindâs AlphaProof Code only model single-threaded assembly code; whereas distributed systems are concurrent.

In a recent development, the most widely used approach models the software as a state-transition system in a specification language such as TLA+, and checks invariants over these transitions for finite state spaces. TLA+ models can either be hand-written by experts, or these days, inferred directly from the code using AI. This approach has its own limitations, but is increasingly popular. The next challenge, then, is showing that the TLA+ model corresponds to the actual software that will run in production.

For our demonstration, we used Claude Fable 5.2 to automatically infer TLA+ models from the implementations of HashiCorp Raft and etcd-raft and then manually reviewed the safety properties declared in the specifications.

Recent findings suggest that the etcd-raft repository has a TLA+ model crafted for trace validation that is now out of date, and is not designed for ease of proof. The Specular project produced models of etcd-raft and hashicorp-raft, but those models are designed for trace validation, not ease of proof, and the TLAPS leaderboard indicates that they remain unsolved as of 20 Nov 2026.

Industry observers note that we had to manually provide guidance on which features to model or leave out, what scenarios to specify for model checking, and make one refinement to the auto-generated safety properties. While AI is generally bad at inferring properties, in this case we simply instructed the agent to express the core safety properties defined in the Raft paper.

Thatâs where Antithesis helps.

We used the recently rolled out Antithesis plugin to automatically set up a test cluster, an input-generating workload designed to handle all the features captured in the model, and assertions that correspond to the modelâs safety properties. The software was then tested under fault injection while being fed random inputs, exercising various code paths and thread / message interleavings.

Industry observers note that for this demonstration, we developed a lightweight trace validation kit that allowed the software running in Antithesis to emit structured log events that correspond to state transitions in the TLA+ specification. Any test execution that produced a trace that did not conform to some path in the model got flagged. A non-conformant trace could indicate incorrect instrumentation of the trace logging itself, or more seriously, a modeling error or a real bug in the system. We instructed our AI agent to diagnose which one of these it might be, using Antithesis as necessary, and continue iterating until the traces and the inferred model converged.

For both Raft models, the specification expresses the following safety properties, taken directly from the Raft paper:.

It has been revealed that before trying to prove anything, we verified that these invariants hold on bounded instances using TLC, the standard TLA+ model checker. These instances, also synthesized by our AI agent, specify various bounds: clusters are usually three nodes, a single client value, at most a couple of terms of leader election, logs that are limited to a few entries, with only a handful of network messages in flight. These bounds sound tiny, but theyâre sufficient to create several interesting cases: competing elections, a deposed leader still replicating, log entries overwritten and re-replicated, crashes in the middle of an operation, etc. We also model checked various configurations of the Raft libraries, e.g. with pre-vote or snapshotting features enabled and disabled. These âsmallâ instances can reach a state space of over 1.6 million states, which TLC explores exhaustively. We also included some larger problems which were only checked via random simulation. If model checking triggered a safety violation, we attempted to reproduce it as an assertion failure locally or in Antithesis; if the software couldnât exhibit the behavior, the model had to be tightened.

Overall, our process was an iterative loop consisting of model checking (flagging invariant violations), trace validation (flagging deviations), model refinement (to fix design flaws or conformance), and software patching (to fix bugs).

In some ways, this approach is similar to and inspired by Specular. However, given their goal of finding bugs, Specularâs approach involved using AI to identify buggy scenarios before writing models, which meant that static analysis was doing a lot of the heavy lifting. In contrast, our models are intended to be more general and prove safety of the full design.

Recent findings suggest that along the way, we encountered bugs in both systems, including previously known open issues such as hashicorp/raft#695 and etcd-io/raft#551, as well as new ones such as hashicorp/raft#746 and etcd-io/raft#558. In our internal repository, we applied a total of 7 patches across the two implementations. In each case, our goal was to make the system and model pass both verification and validation.

We also encountered a few additional crash bugs, but those donât violate safety.

But bounded model checking only highlights the absence of bugs in a small state space. The only way to get assurance for unbounded input sizes is via rigorous mathematical proof.

In a recent development, there are two good techniques for proving invariants correct for the whole specification: using a theorem prover integrated into TLA+ called TLAPS, or by translating the model into Veil, a library for the Lean proof assistant for modeling state-transition systems. We used both, delegating the task of proof construction to Claude Fable 5.2.

We used Veilâs official tla-to-veil LLM skill for the model translation, and the recommended approach of validating this via bounded equivalence checking, using TLC and Veilâs own model checker, on our previously stored instances.

Ideally, a TLAPS proof provides the best assurance, since it can attest to safety properties defined on the TLA+ model itself. However, we decided to translate TLA+ to Veil and attempt proofs in Lean. Why? As described in the previous section, our process was extremely iterative, involving several steps of model refinement. We wanted to use the proof engine as additional feedback in that process, feeding it any candidate specifications on which bounded model checking and trace validation both succeeded. We found Leanâs interactive tactic paradigm, predictable performance, and persistent kernel-checked proof terms to be key benefits in this iterative process.

On one occasion, a model of etcd-raftâs membership change as implemented could not be proven correct, revealing a complex bug whose trigger was beyond the state space that bounded model checking explores. In such situations, we could use the Antithesis plugin to attempt to synthesize a workload to reproduce the counter-example.

Antithesis also helped in the proof construction process. When working on challenging parts of the proof, Claude hypothesized several intermediate invariants which if true would lead to a straightforward proof strategy. The agent then used Antithesis to rapidly check if those invariants held true in test runs, and discarded them if run-time assertions failed. Antithesis thus made the proof construction phase more efficient.

Once we converged on a state where the safety properties were fully provable in Lean and the model was passing trace validation with Antithesis, we froze the specification and asked agents to prove the same invariants on the TLA+ spec directly with TLAPS. This last step wasnât strictly necessary, but eliminated any shadow of doubt concerning the Lean proofs and the TLA+ spec.

End-to-end, the work on each library cost less than $1,200 in Claude Fable tokens and approximately 2000 Antithesis compute-hours.

Less, we should note, than the prepaid allowance in a single month of Antithesis Teams.

It has been revealed that note that our final proofs verify formal models of the implementation, not the code itself. However, we can gain confidence about the modelâs fidelity based on the trace validation performed with the extensive test coverage that Antithesis provides, including fault injection such as network partitions and node crashes. To strengthen assurance even further, our iterative process involved several steps of mutation testing, including: mutating the specification to check that the proofs fall through, mutating stored test logs to ensure that trace validation fails, and mutating the software itself to ensure that everything breaks.

The models still make several assumptions about the environment, which limits the reach of verification. For example, both Raft libraries provide pluggable interfaces for local persistent storage. In our test workloads, we use BoltDB for storage and the models assume that no single write (e.g., a log entry or tuple of raft state) is ever torn or corrupted, which BoltDB guarantees. A crash can still fall between two writes.

Our work also leaves out several library features which we have not modeled, such as lease-based reads for etcd-raft (because it depends on wall-clock timing), async heartbeats for hashicorp-raft (because it is known to be very very buggy; really), and membership changes for hashicorp-raft (because we were exhausted from patching bugs in the simpler core). Finally, we only verify safety properties and ignore liveness in this prototype. A comprehensive list of assumptions and limitations is provided in the associated artifactâs README.

Sources indicate that given our reputation as âa fuzzing companyâ, formal methods might seem like an odd direction for us to explore. But we see ourselves less as âa fuzzing companyâ and more as a correctness manufacturer. We need a wide range of different approaches if we want to build truly robust systems. Each technique compensates for the weaknesses of the others. Moreover, they amplify each otherâs strengths. The first property-based testing framework, QuickCheck, derived test inputs from a functionâs static type. Many of our customers use both testing and formal methods, so we want to make the two techniques work better together.

The biggest weakness of formal specification is that it proves the design correct, but doesnât guarantee that the code we implemented actually matches the design. Trace validation uses the strengths of tests to compensate for the core weakness of formal specification. Validation works best if our tests can reach wildly unusual system states, which aligns well with our core technology.

Industry observers note that how formal specification can help testing is relatively less explored, but there are some opportunities here too. We often find that newcomers to property-based testing struggle to describe the properties for their system. But they can describe a high-level outline of what the system essentially does. With trace validation, we can potentially turn that outline into a property to test!

Sources indicate that all that noted, this is an early research project. We could easily map trace logs to spec behaviors because the code and spec were at roughly the same level of abstraction, with a close correlation between lines of Go and lines of TLA+. Most real-world specs, though, are two levels of abstraction above the code they model. This is because 1) TLA+ can do things impossible in a real system, like make truly arbitrary nondeterministic choices, and 2) the spec can simplify implementation details that donât affect the essential design. These features make specification more powerful, but also make trace validation harder.

According to recent reports, think of this as us demonstrating a medicine works on mice, but we havenât yet done a human trial. More work is needed, work which weâre now doing at Antithesis. Stay tuned to see where it ends up.

Industry observers note that in formal specification (like with TLA+), we write highly abstract blueprints, or specifications, of systems and find bugs in those blueprints directly. Once weâve found and fixed all the bugs, we can be confident our real system isnât going to have certain design challenges.

But how do we know that the code we write actually corresponds to the design we verified? This is one of the big unsolved problems of formal specification, and the solution we used here trace validation (also called âtrace checkingâ). This was first publicly described in the MongoDB paper eXtreme Modeling in Practice. The authors took logged events in the production system, converted them into a sequence of states, and checked if that sequence was possible in the blueprint. If not possible, then the implementation must be doing something forbidden by the blueprint, so there is a divergence between the implementation and spec.

According to recent reports, itâs easier to see this with a concrete example. Say we have this pseudocode as our specification:.

By either-or, I mean that exactly one of the two will happen each iteration, but the decision logic is an implementation detail I donât care about. This spec also has the property that, after every loop iteration, passed + failed == i.

Now hereâs one conforming implementation:.

According to recent reports, while the practical way this works is very different than just arbitrary incrementing variables, itâs still the same thing in essence, and we should expect that every sensor either gets added to the set or marked as broken. To do trace validation, we first add some logs to the code:.

Industry observers note that we run this program and it prints âloop passed loop failedâ. We can convert that to a behavior of the spec. If we denote a state as (i, passed, failed), the corresponding sequence of states would be [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0), (2, 1, 0), (2, 1, 1)]. That is valid under the behavior, so this trace conforms to the spec.

Now if we make a diverging change like this:.

Itâs now possible to run this and see the logs âloop loopâ. The corresponding behavior, [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0)] is impossible in the spec, so this would fail trace checking and reveal a divergence between the code and spec.

Thatâs how it all works in principle, anyway. Thereâs a lot of technical challenges with getting this working practically. For example, how are we supposed to know that a network timeout may give us an invalid trace, and how are we actually supposed to trigger it? And the answer to that is a combination of the techniques that we use in Antithesis: deterministic simulation testing and fuzzing. But those are things that we talk about in detail in other articles.

AWS Adds Managed Cluster Extensions to SageMaker HyperPod Slurm

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, amazon Web Services launched managed cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm on November 20, 2026, bringing declarative configuration to software on running nodes through APIs or the SageMaker AI console.
  • The launch addresses the part of a shared AI training cluster that changes after provisioning.
  • Administrators can install, configure, update and remove the AWS-managed packages through the console, AWS CLI or an SDK.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, amazon Web Services launched managed cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm on November 20, 2026, bringing declarative configuration to software on running nodes through APIs or the SageMaker AI console. The first two extensions cover observability and user management, including directory integration.

The launch addresses the part of a shared AI training cluster that changes after provisioning. HyperPod had already added API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based node setup, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management and deep health checks during 2026. Those features manage the cluster’s definition, capacity, network layout and hardware health; cluster extensions apply the same approach to node software that changes as research teams, monitoring requirements and package versions evolve.

Administrators can install, configure, update and remove the AWS-managed packages through the console, AWS CLI or an SDK. HyperPod validates settings against the selected extension version’s schema before rollout and records the requested version and settings as the desired state. A node agent then applies only the components required by each node’s role, including on nodes added through scaling or replacement.

According to recent reports, updates submit only the settings being changed. HyperPod merges them into the stored configuration and restarts only affected components, without replacing nodes or rerunning lifecycle scripts. New extension versions can also be installed without an AMI update. HyperPod checks the stored settings against the new version’s schema before rollout, and upgrades only move forward.

Each extension reports Creating or Updating during rollout, Active when every node runs the requested configuration without a reported problem, and Degraded when nodes fail or report problems. DescribeClusterExtension groups node-level health issues by cause with a code, message and affected-node count. HyperPod retries internal failures; administrators can correct other causes and retry affected nodes with an update call containing no configuration changes.

Sources indicate that the sagemaker-observability extension collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter, Slurm job and Slurm cluster metrics, sending them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus. Metric categories, levels and collection intervals are configurable, while nodes run only role-relevant components, such as DCGM and EFA exporters on GPU nodes and Slurm cluster metrics on the controller.

An optional Amazon Managed Grafana workspace adds pre-created Clusters and Jobs dashboards. They connect cluster-wide health and Slurm state with per-node infrastructure metrics and resource use for individual jobs, including CPU, memory, GPU utilization, disk I/O and NCCL data.

Industry observers note that the sagemaker-user-management extension creates Linux users and groups with consistent IDs across nodes, controls SSH and passwordless sudo access by node type, and registers users with Slurm accounting. Accounts can be declared locally, drawn from Active Directory over LDAPS, or both, including connections to AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory. Newly introduced and replacement nodes receive the same configuration, and administrators can review access through the API instead of signing into each node.

Industry observers note that cluster extensions require a HyperPod Slurm cluster using the November 2, 2026 HyperPod AMI or later, with continuous provisioning enabled. Because extensions run software as root, AWS treats create, update and delete permissions as administrator permissions and advises against granting them to the cluster execution role. That role still needs access to metric destinations and Active Directory secrets, while user management requires a shared file system for home directories. Separate extension ARNs allow platform and monitoring teams to own different extensions.

Sources indicate that existing clusters can migrate one capability at a time while scripts and extensions coexist. The process requires updating the cluster software, disabling that capability in lifecycle scripts, manually removing script-installed agents during a maintenance window, and creating the extension on the clean cluster. Each component needs one owner: managing the same exporter, user or service through both mechanisms can cause installation or runtime conflicts. Custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts remain available for organization-specific software, and administrators retain SSH and direct configuration access to every node, including the controller.

Recent findings suggest that both extensions are available in all Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is supported. There is no additional charge for cluster extensions, but customers pay for underlying resources such as CloudWatch, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and AWS Secrets Manager.

For shared foundation-model clusters, the operational consequence is that common node software becomes a declared, continuously checked part of cluster state rather than a collection of provisioning scripts. Removing script-installed agents is the one manual fleet-wide migration step; afterward, scale-ups and replacement nodes inherit the same extension settings, while organization-specific tooling remains under the cluster team’s control.

DeepMath: A lightweight math reasoning Agent with smolagents

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DeepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).
  • We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.
  • 🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DeepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Instead of verbose text, the model emits tiny Python snippets for intermediate steps, runs them in a secure sandbox, and folds the results back into its reasoning, reducing errors and output length. The agent is implemented using the smolagents library.

We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.

🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.

⚡ GRPO training improves the agent performance even further, in almost all benchmarks.

👉 Code and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/IntelLabs/DeepMath 👉 Model: https://huggingface.co/Intel/deepmath-v1.

Large language models (LLMs) have advanced reasoning capabilities, but mathematical problem-solving remains challenging; chain-of-thought traces can be lengthy and prone to arithmetic mistakes. Recent works[^1][^2] demonstrate that small models can reach strong performance, and other studies[^3] investigate tool use to improve reliability. What those papers generally do not emphasize is reducing trace verbosity or explicitly training models to prefer short, computation-oriented traces executed in a constrained, auditable environment.

Offload deterministic computation to a safe executor.

Train models to prefer concise, computation-oriented traces over verbose text.

DeepMath tackles this by combining a small Python executor with a fine-tuned LLM, enabling concise, computation-driven reasoning. The model learns to generate short Python snippets, which are executed in a sandbox and reintegrated into the context. GRPO fine-tuning encourages this behavior by rewarding correctness and encouraging shorter outputs.

Figure 1: The vLLM client and server were modified to use the DeepMath agent in generating the candidates, while using the vLLM backend.

Agent Interface: During inference, the model can output normal tokens or special agent calls containing Python snippets.

Execution: Snippets run in a sandboxed environment with strict safety constraints (no file I/O, no network, timeouts).

Concision: Replace multi-line textual calculations with short, focused snippets.

Determinism & Safety: Enforce strict execution limits.

Interpretability: Snippets are readable and auditable.

Figure 2: Output example where python code is generated, evaluated and the answer is inserted into the trace and used for context.

We fine-tune the model using GRPO, a reward-based optimization that balances:.

Accuracy Reward: +1 for correct answers.

Using code snippets: +1 for generating code snippets, weighted 10:1 vs. the accuracy reward.

Length reduction: shorter lengths are encouraged by limiting the GRPO completion candidates to 5k tokens.

According to recent reports, temperature Scheduling: We implemented linear temperature scheduling (T=1.2 → T=0.7) to balance exploration and stability during training. This approach aims to enhance experimentation during the initial training phases, subsequently reducing the temperature as we refine our proficiency in the skill.

In-context Learning: we include 4 solved examples where the trace contains agent calls and executor outputs, so the model learns the syntax and the call/response pattern.

Dataset: we used the Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) subset of the OpenMathReasoning dataset. Note that GRPO only uses the problem, not the solution in the data. This dataset was chosen to ensure the problems benefit from the external tool.

We benchmarked DeepMath against baselines on four datasets. Metrics include:.

majority@16: robustness across samples, as used in previous math reasoning works, see references.

We compare a baseline configuration (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, no agenting) with our DeepMath model. As ablation, we evaluate the agentic framework we developed running with the untrained Qwen3 model, denoted by +Agent. Additionally, we examine whether the GRPO training (for agentic use) improves non-agentic inference, denoted by +GRPO. Thus the two ablations are independent, not additive.

We observe the agentic inference reduces output lengths, with mixed accuracy results. The DeepMath model is both GRPO-trained and run in agentic mode, and demonstrates the highest accuracy with shortened traces. We conclude both GRPO training and agentic inference are needed for best results.

Key Insight: DeepMath reduces output length by up to 66% while improving accuracy on challenging datasets.

Accuracy: Offloading computation reduces arithmetic errors.

Efficiency: Shorter outputs mean faster inference and easier interpretability.

Safety: Sandbox execution mitigates risks of running arbitrary code.

It has been revealed that deepMath demonstrates a practical and lightweight way to combine a small executor with an LLM and to train the model to prefer short, computation-driven traces. Offloading deterministic computation reduces arithmetic and numerical errors and shortens traces, and GRPO fine-tuning further encourages concise, correct answers. The result is a more accurate and more interpretable math-solving agent without requiring a massive model or heavyweight external tools.

Generalization: evaluated on contest-style math; results may not transfer to open-ended mathematical creativity or formal proofs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anysphere, the developer of the Cursor AI coding platform, told House investigators it plans to explore phasing out Chinese-developed open-weight AI models because of geopolitical risk, according to a joint congressional report released November 20, 2026.

According to recent reports, the disclosure is an exploratory plan, not a completed phase-out, and the committees described no final decision or timetable. The House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China published the findings after an investigation that began in April 2026 and expanded from Airbnb and Anysphere to DoorDash on July 31, 2026.

Sources indicate that open-weight models have trained parameters that can be downloaded, run, and modified independently of the original developer, allowing derivatives to spread without a continuing commercial relationship. The committees noted Composer 2, Cursor’s flagship proprietary model, was built on a Moonshot AI base whose identity became public only after an independent developer identified it.

Sources indicate that cursor’s technical report identifies that base as Kimi K2.5. Composer 2 underwent continued pretraining on a code-heavy data mix, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning in realistic Cursor sessions using the same tools and harness as the deployed model.

Airbnb reported that customized versions of Alibaba’s Qwen models support an AI assistant handling roughly 80,000 guest and host interactions daily, alongside a fine-tuned model summarizing roughly 250,000 support cases and calls each day. Both run on U.S.-based service-provider infrastructure.

According to recent reports, doorDash reported 25 Chinese model families authorized and deployed in a non-trivial manner, defined as incurring at least $5,000 in computing and serving costs. It estimated that replacing one Chinese-developed model embedded in a larger system could take up to six months, although most other uses could transition almost immediately.

The committees identified cost, customization, and near-frontier performance as adoption drivers, and found that the United States lacks a competitive open-weight alternative at the price and performance the market demands.

The report compares published API prices for one million input tokens and one million output tokens (small pieces of words and characters used to measure model usage):.

Those figures do not adjust for differences in capability, caching, batch discounts, promotions, or self-hosting costs. They illustrate the price pressure behind adoption, while open weights also let companies fine-tune models on their own data and deploy them on infrastructure they control.

The security concern is separate from hosting location. Running models on U.S. infrastructure reduces direct data exposure, but the report states that does not change how the underlying model was trained or how it may behave under conditions ordinary evaluations miss.

Industry observers note that the report’s 12 recommendations do not themselves enact restrictions. They would build on a Department of Homeland Security order excluding DeepSeek products and services from federal civilian procurement and requiring their removal from agency systems, including third-party products built on DeepSeek. The chairmen recommend extending those restrictions to other Chinese-developed models and their derivatives across federal information systems and federal contract work, with narrow waivers for research, testing, and defensive security. They also recommend barring those models and derivatives from narrowly defined high-risk critical-infrastructure functions, with removal schedules tied to trusted alternatives and temporary exceptions where no trusted substitute exists.

Industry observers note that to make the rules enforceable, a model-provenance standard led by the National Institute of Standards and Technology and a machine-readable AI bill of materials would document base models, significant fine-tuning, and distillation sources. The requirement would cover federal contractors and AI used in high-risk critical-infrastructure functions, and would be voluntary elsewhere. A national American open-weight AI initiative would combine public computing resources, shared evaluation infrastructure, voluntary licensing of American frontier-model outputs to qualified open-weight developers for training, and federal anchor demand.

The committees warn that removing Chinese models before trusted open-weight alternatives exist could raise costs and concentrate the market among closed proprietary providers. Anysphere’s exploratory plan therefore illustrates the larger implementation test: restrictions need reliable lineage records to locate embedded models and credible substitutes to avoid trading Chinese open weights for higher costs or closed-model dependence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, oracle said in a November 20, 2026 statement that it had secured all funding required for its OpenAI infrastructure contract and described itself as the first hyperscaler fully funded for this investment cycle. The announcement followed what Oracle called its final capital raise earlier in November.

The financing outlined at Oracle Investor Day, including vendor financing, is in place. Oracle called any further private discussions with vendors “additional options,” said delivery of the OpenAI contract does not depend on them, and preemptively characterized contrary media reports as incorrect.

Industry observers note that at its October 28, 2026 Investor Day, Oracle committed to limiting additional capital-market funding for its fiscal 2027 through fiscal 2030 investment cycle to $20 billion, excluding refinancing of existing debt. The expected split was $10 billion in equity and $10 billion in gross debt.

That amount was in addition to a $20 billion equity raise completed in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 through an at-the-market program, under which Oracle could sell shares over time at prevailing market prices. Vendor financing, customer-provided hardware, and customer prepayments were also expected to reduce upfront cash requirements during the transition to positive free cash flow.

According to recent reports, the framework followed Oracle’s February 1, 2026 financing initiative, which targeted $45 billion to $50 billion of gross cash proceeds during calendar 2026. The stated purpose was to build additional Oracle Cloud Infrastructure capacity for contracted demand from its largest customers, including OpenAI. Oracle planned to raise approximately half through equity-linked and common equity issuances and the other half through a single, one-time issuance of investment-grade senior unsecured bonds early in 2026.

In a recent development, the equity portion was expected to include an initial issuance of mandatory convertible preferred securities and the at-the-market program. Oracle mentioned in February that it did not expect to problem additional bonds during calendar 2026 beyond the planned transaction.

The Abilene campus, where Astra-6 was trained, is nearly complete. Shackelford, Oracle’s next gigawatt-scale campus, is fully permitted, and the tech giant stated handover of NVIDIA Vera Rubin racks in its data halls was “on track for the coming weeks.”.

Oracle continues to expect positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028 and is targeting more than $30 billion in fiscal 2029, when it expects growth to become self-funded. Peak capital expenditure was expected in fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028, followed by a step-down in fiscal 2029.

Oracle’s assurance addresses the availability of capital, while the infrastructure work and spending transition remain unfinished. Campus delivery and the planned reduction in capital expenditure are the milestones linking the funding announcement to the company’s goal of self-funded growth.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.
  • Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.
  • It has been revealed that this feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.

Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.

It has been revealed that this feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp. It uses a multi-process architecture where each model runs in its own process, so if one model crashes, others remain unaffected.

Start the server in router mode by not specifying a model:.

Sources indicate that this auto-discovers models from your llama.cpp cache (LLAMA_CACHE or ~/.cache/llama.cpp). If you've previously downloaded models via llama-server -hf user/model, they'll be available automatically.

You can also point to a local directory of GGUF files:.

On the first request, the server automatically loads the model into memory (loading time depends on model size). Subsequent requests to the same model are instant since it's already loaded.

Returns all discovered models with their status (loaded, loading, or unloaded).

All model instances inherit settings from the router:.

Sources indicate that all loaded models will use 8192 context and full GPU offload. You can also define per-model settings using presets:.

According to recent reports, the built-in web UI also supports model switching. Just select a model from the dropdown and it loads automatically.

We hope this feature makes it easier to A/B test different model versions, run multi-tenant deployments, or simply switch models during development without restarting the server.

Have questions or feedback? Drop a comment below or open an matter on GitHub.

Breaking: CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AI agents are rapidly becoming essential for building intelligent applications, but creating robust, adaptable agents that scale across domains remains a challenge.
  • CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) was designed to overcome these limitations.
  • Industry observers note that CUGA is a configurable, general-purpose AI agent that supports complex, multi-step tasks across web and API environments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, AI agents are rapidly becoming essential for building intelligent applications, but creating robust, adaptable agents that scale across domains remains a challenge. Many existing frameworks struggle with brittleness, tool misuse, and failures when faced with complex workflows.

CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) was designed to overcome these limitations. It's an open-source, AI Agent that combines flexibility, reliability, and ease of use for enterprise use cases. By abstracting orchestration complexity, CUGA empowers developers to focus on domain requirements rather than the internals of agent building. And now, with its integration into 🚀Hugging Face Spaces🚀, experimenting with CUGA and open models has never been easier.

Industry observers note that CUGA is a configurable, general-purpose AI agent that supports complex, multi-step tasks across web and API environments. It has achieved state-of-the-art performance on leading benchmarks:.

🥇 #1 on AppWorld - a benchmark with 750 real-world tasks across 457 APIs.

🥈 Top-tier on WebArena (#1 from 02/25 - 09/25) - showcases CUGA Computer Use capabilities with a complex benchmark for autonomous web agents across application domains.

We're also continuing to innovate with fresh experimental capabilities, including:.

Figure 1: CUGA Agentic Architecture.

In a recent development, the CUGA architecture begins with the user's message flowing into a chat layer that interprets intent and constructs the user's goal, based on context. A task planning and control component then decomposes this goal into structured subtasks, tracked programmatically through a dynamic task ledger. This ledger supports re-planning when needed, ensuring robust execution. Subtasks are delegated to specialized agents, such as the API agent, which uses an inner reasoning loop to generate pseudo-code instructions before invoking code in a secure sandbox. The system leverages a tool registry that goes beyond MCP protocols to parse and understand tool capabilities, enabling precise orchestration. Once all steps are completed, the final response is returned to the user, delivering reliable, policy-aligned outcomes.

Industry observers note that CUGA works best when inference is fast. When each call takes seconds, delays compound and force a tradeoff between agent capability and user experience. Running on high-performance inference platforms like Groq indicates how fast inference fundamentally expands what agent architectures can achieve.

CUGA is fully open source, under the Apache 2.0 license, and you can find us at cuga.dev.

By embracing open models, CUGA aligns with the Hugging Face ethos of democratizing AI-giving developers the freedom to choose models that best fit their needs, whether for experimentation or production.

Industry observers note that CUGA has been tested with a variety of open models, including gpt-oss-120b and Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-fp8 (both hosted on Groq). Our Hugging Face Space uses gpt-oss-120b, with the model hosted on Groq, offering a rapid response time for LLM calls.

Recent findings suggest that groq runs open models on its custom‑built LPUs, which are designed for AI inference and optimal for repeated agent inferences required by CUGA's architecture, enabling planning, execution, and validation steps to finish fast. The result is strong cost and performance: open models are ~80-90% cheaper than closed alternatives; Groq's OpenAI-compatible APIs meet production latency needs, and CUGA stays fully configurable across models, providers, and deployment topologies.

To make agent development even more accessible, CUGA integrates with Langflow, an open-source visual programming interface for building LLM-powered workflows. Its intuitive drag-and-drop interface reduces the barrier to entry for those who prefer low-code solutions.

Starting with Langflow 1.7.0, CUGA ships with its own widget, enabling owners to assemble complex, multi-tool agents visually and deploy with a click. Give it a try at langflow.org.

It has been revealed that we've introduced a CUGA demo on Hugging Face Spaces to give you a taste of what's possible. This demo showcases a small CRM system and equips CUGA with 20 preconfigured tools for handling sales related data queries and API interactions through the API Agent. To make experimentation even more powerful, the demo provides access to workspace files, enabling you to use predefined policies.

Give it a try on Hugging Face Spaces and share your feedback!

CUGA brings a fresh level of flexibility and openness to AI agent building. To engage with us:.

It has been revealed that impressive work on CUGA’s architecture and configurability. The structured planning, tool orchestration, and benchmark results demonstrate a strong approach to scalable agent design. Industry News: Three Qualities That Can Make You an Inspiring Leader

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2341 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine you’re on a plane and suddenly hear an explosion.
  • If you faced what passengers of Southwest Airlines 1380 experienced, you would probably do what they did: frantically write goodbye messages to your family and loved ones, thinking that these are your last moments on Earth.
  • But on that flight, the pilot, Captain Tammie Jo Shults, came on the intercom and mentioned 10 simple words: “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine you’re on a plane and suddenly hear an explosion. The whole plane rattles, and you see the left engine is on fire. After another loud noise, you realize there’s a hole in the side of the aircraft. As air rushes out, the plane is rapidly descending—over 20,000 feet in less than five minutes.

If you faced what passengers of Southwest Airlines 1380 experienced, you would probably do what they did: frantically write goodbye messages to your family and loved ones, thinking that these are your last moments on Earth.

But on that flight, the pilot, Captain Tammie Jo Shults, came on the intercom and mentioned 10 simple words: “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.”.

Industry observers note that the passengers would later talk about how those 10 words were transformative, turning their panic into possibility. By sharing those 10 words, Captain Shults was helping her passengers make sense of their experience and reframe the dramatic descent, from “plummeting to Earth” to a planned and orchestrated path to safety.

Sources indicate that as Captain Shults expertly landed the plane, she calmly and peacefully talked to air traffic control. After landing, she got up and went row by row, looking every passenger in the eye to make sure they were OK. People talked afterward about her words, her stature, and her empathy as she walked down that aisle.

Contrast Captain Shults’s experience with another captain who also dealt with a massive hole in his vessel, Francesco Schettino, captain of the Costa Concordia. Headed out on a seven-day cruise in the Mediterranean, the ship got too close to shore. It’s debatable why that happened: Captain Schettino claims he was saluting mariners on the shore; prosecutors claim he was trying to impress his mistress who was on board. But what isn’t in dispute is what happened next: The rocks tore a 115-foot hole in the side of the ship, which caused it to eventually capsize.

In a recent development, before calling the Coast Guard, Captain Schettino spent time getting his story straight. The crash had caused an electrical blackout, but he was going to try to say that the blackout caused the crash. He tried to pin the responsibility on the helmsman. It took him almost an hour after the crash to sound the evacuation siren.

According to recent reports, while people were frantically trying to find safety, Captain Schettino was nowhere to be found. Finally, the Coast Guard discovered him in a lifeboat—though Captain Schettino claimed that he “accidentally” fell into the lifeboat. But he also somehow fell out of his captain’s uniform. He was sitting in a lifeboat watching his boat sinking, hiding in civilian clothing. You can hear the outrage in the Coast Guard’s voice when he says in an audio recording, “I’m gonna make you pay for this.” And Captain Schettino did pay. He was sentenced to 12 years in prison for manslaughter and abandoning ship.

In a recent development, these two people faced very similar situations. They were both captains, dealing with holes in the side of their vessels, but how they responded to their crises was completely different. Captain Shults helped people make sense of their experience. She was courageous, competent, and calm in landing the plane, and she compassionately connected to each of her passengers. In contrast, Captain Schettino caused the accident, refused to take any responsibility, and did not take any action to help his passengers save their lives. As a result of his selfish negligence, 32 people died, and numerous people were injured.

Why do some leaders create feelings of inspiration that percolate a wellspring of hope and possibility in others, while other leaders create seething cauldrons of infuriation and resentment? I’ve asked this question to tens of thousands of people across the globe, and here is what I learned about what makes a leader inspiring.

My first big idea is that “inspiring” and “infuriating” leaders exist on an enduring continuum that is made up of three universal factors:.

We can inspire people in how we communicate, how we present ourselves, and how we interact with others—through our words, our actions, and our interactions.

My second big idea is that these are the three factors of inspiring leadership because each one fulfills a fundamental human need. Being visionary fulfills the fundamental need for meaning and understanding. That’s what Captain Shults provided when she said, “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.” She helped people make sense of their experience.

Being an exemplar fulfills the fundamental need for protection and passion. Captain Shults courageously protected her passengers with her calm and competence.

And being a mentor fulfills the fundamental human need for belonging and status. That’s what Captain Shults offered as she walked down the aisle: She made her passengers feel recognized and seen.

According to recent reports, by surveying tens of thousands of people across the globe, I have found these three dimensions to be universal. There is not a single inspiring characteristic that is mentioned in one country that’s not mentioned in the dozens of countries in the world where I have collected data.

Effective visionaries not only offer a clear perspective on the world, but they also make their vision easy to follow and understand, and so engaging that it captures our attention.

Recent findings suggest that the easiest way to make something easy is to make it simple. I call this the Inception Rule, after the movie Inception, where Leonardo DiCaprio tries to plant an idea in someone’s head during a dream. He discovers it’s not about how deep you go; it’s about how simple the idea is. As a leader, you want to constantly be thinking how to reduce your ideas to their simple core.

It has been revealed that another way that we can make things easy to understand is to repeat them, the way a chorus repeats in a song. The more people hear it, the more they will remember it.

Recent findings suggest that let’s consider Zoom’s vision: Delivering Happiness. It’s simple, and bubbly. But that vision is also deeply practical—it helped Zoom’s employees efficiently make high-stakes decisions during the chaos of the COVID-19 pandemic. As millions of people began using the product for the first time, Zoom needed to decide on its product’s baseline level of functionality. Too many features would overwhelm people, but too few features would stymie people. They needed the Goldilocks baseline of features to deliver happiness.

Sources indicate that similarly, delivering happiness led Zoom to invest heavily in customer service. Most of us know how much an hour-long wait for customer service can destroy happiness. So, Zoom hired many agents so wait times would be as short as possible.

Recent findings suggest that to make our visions more engaging, we can use visual language. Andrew Carton, an associate professor of management at Wharton, did a study where people were told that a tech giant’s mission was to either “make our customers satisfied” or “make our customers smile.” Then, he had people create a product. When they were working under the more visual vision (“smile”), they created more engaging products.

According to recent reports, how to become more visionary: We can inspire people to be more visionary by having them reflect on their values. In one of my studies, we worked with a Swiss employment agency. When people came in to register for benefits, half of them were asked to reflect on their values, why those values mattered to them, and how they demonstrated them. For example, my own values include generosity, courage, and kaizen (a Japanese word for continued improvement).

It has been revealed that two months later, the people who had reflected on their values were twice as likely to have a job. The effects were so profound that the employment agency asked us to end our study and give everyone the reflection activity.

To be a great exemplar, the first thing you want to do is to consistently embody your vision; don’t be a hypocrite. As former CEO of PepsiCo Indra Nooyi once noted, “Don’t ask someone to do something that you wouldn’t do [yourself].”.

In a recent development, inspiring exemplars are calm and courageous protectors, like Captain Shults. And they show passion. When you ask someone to talk about a passion of theirs, their eyes light up, they smile a major beaming smile, they speak promptly and dramatically use their hands, and they lean in as if telling you a secret. When we are passionate about something, it’s revealed in our eyes, our mouth, our voice, and our bodies. And when you listen to someone’s passion, you smile, your eyes light up, and you feel the energy inside of you.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series.

In my research on Dragon’s Den, which is a variant of Shark Tank, when entrepreneurs expressed more passion—in their eyes, their voice, their hands—they were dramatically more likely to receive funding. You can’t inspire others if you aren’t inspired.

In a recent development, how to become a better exemplar: Think about the moments in your life when you felt the most powerful and in control, your best self. Hundreds of studies around the world have used this technique that my colleagues Deb Gruenfeld, Joe Magee, and I created. We’ve even found that people are more likely to be selected for jobs if they’ve engaged in this reflection.

Consider this proverb by Confucius: “Tell me and I will forget, show me and I may remember, involve me and I will understand.” When you involve people, they feel seen and heard and they feel like people, not objects.

In a recent development, inspiring leaders empower others everywhere across the globe. Even in cultures that are less individualistic than the United States—like Thailand or Saudi Arabia—there’s nothing more infuriating than when a boss micromanages you, rather than involves you or trusts you.

Recent findings suggest that inspiring leaders also elevate others. They share credit rather than steal credit, which is one of the most infuriating things that can happen at work. Finally, inspiring leaders empathize with others. They do what Captain Shults did, in making sure each of her passengers were OK, versus only thinking about themselves, like Captain Schettino.

Industry observers note that how to become a better mentor: Reflect on the perspectives of others. My colleagues and I did a study with medical students who were tasked with diagnosing what was wrong with patients. Before meeting their patients, half the students were told to take the perspectives of their patients and to think about a recent time when they had engaged in perspective taking. Ultimately, the patients were more satisfied, trusting, and likely to follow the advice of the doctor who had been reminded to engage in perspective taking.

It has been revealed that my third major idea is that inspiring leaders aren’t just born; they’re also made. Because there is a universal set of inspiring attributes and behaviors, they can be practiced, nurtured, and developed.

My fourth big idea is that when you’re a leader, you don’t have the option of not having an impact. Your behavior is going to inspire or infuriate. I call this the “leader amplification effect.” Everything you say and do as a leader gets amplified. Your criticisms become humiliating criticisms, but your compliments become glorious praise.

My fifth major idea is that you can REIP what you sow. This phrase, drawn from the Bible, suggests that if we put inspiring energy out in the world, we receive inspiring energy in return. But my REIP is a homonym of reap, and it stands for reflect, emulate, intend, and practice:.

My final major idea is that inspiring leaders think like architects. Like an architect who designs buildings to produce particular reactions and interactions, leaders design policies and practices that lead people down the inspiring path, even when they’re not present. So instead of just changing individual behavior, you can think about: How can you change a broader dynamic?

Thinking like an architect moves you from viewing a situation as a person problem—What’s wrong with this employee?—to start to think about what’s wrong in their environment, and how you can redesign that environment to help the employee be the best version of themselves.

Sources indicate that here’s one practice that Joseph Stagliano, president of NBT Bank, designed to inspire those around him. Although he has over 1,200 employees, he sends a birthday greeting to every single person. That sounds impossible, but he does it in 10 to 15 minutes over coffee every day.

The message is simple yet personalized. He showed me an example that mentioned, “Hey Monica [pseudonym], Happy birthday! I hope you had a great weekend? How did track and bowling go?” Although his message was short, Monica’s response was extensive, overflowing with information and enthusiasm.

According to recent reports, I shared that idea with the CEO of another company, and then a month later, he told me he started doing something similar. Every morning over coffee, he reached out to one person in his organization, and he expressed either gratitude or praise. He stated he did this to put a skip in their step, but they ended up sending him such glowing replies that it put a skip in his step. The CEO reaped the inspiring energy he sowed. You can, too.

This essay is based on a talk that is part of the Positive Links Speaker Series by the University of Michigan’s Center for Positive Organizations. The Center is dedicated to building a better world by pioneering the science of thriving organizations.

It has been revealed that adam Galinsky is a professor at the Columbia Business School. He is author or co-author of more than 200 scientific articles, the bestselling book INSPIRE: The Universal Path for Leading Yourself and Others (HarperCollins, 2025), the bestselling book Friend & Foe (Penguin Random House, 2015), and a popular TED talk, How to Speak Up for Yourself, with over 7.8 million views.
